title: Start here
text: A small farm, built one working loop at a time. The current plan in one place: build the farm software on the Mac now, then connect and commission the robot in Japan from September 30. Open the step-by-step guide Read the software roadmap Assemble the robot Done · Sep 27 The farm program exists Adapters, LLM-taught skills, perception, care cycle, evidence store, viewer with STOP, Jev/Astra authority ladder, Telegram, run recording. 37 tests pass; real-model checks done. software/ Next · Japan Commission one care cycle Park the robot. Inspect, measure, make a supervised bottle pour, verify the outcome and recover from interruptions. Later · gated Earn more autonomy Task demonstrations, held-out evaluation, longer observation windows and only then additional care or mobility. Status, September 27: no planter parts have been printed and no growing test has happened (the NY K1 Max jammed). The printer now available is an AnkerMake M5C (220 × 220 × 250 mm): the cress planter and the new nest/paddle/bottle-rest parts fit; the square kit's 220 mm outer tray does not. The farm software is written and tested on its simulator; hardware validation starts when the robot is assembled on September 30. Nobody drives the robot: motion is taught by the vision model, decisions go rules → Jev → a person only when needed. What we have decided Topic Current direction Status Watering A small robot-held pouring bottle. Human refill. Chosen; grip/spout and accurate pours untested. Growing Rectangular wicking planter and square covered germination kit. Each can finish a crop. Not printed yet; printer jammed. No leak/wick test has been done. Sensing One removable light paddle. Moisture probe and relay deferred for paper trays. Recommended first build; human water/wetness checks before refills. Cameras Use the robot’s head/wrist cameras initially. No separate overhead camera in the first build. Computer The Mac connects to robot interfaces, cameras and ESP32 through the owned powered USB hub. Physical connections still to commission. Battery Anker C300 DC received. Not used in V0; robot runs on its wall supplies while parked. 12 V harness from the car outlet still undesigned and unfused. Furniture Free fully printed modular table for the planters; separate cart for the robot. Table chosen; editable model files still missing. Software Eight-layer farm program on the Mac over LeRobot 0.6: adapters, LLM-servo skills, perception, care cycle, evidence, viewer, Jev/Astra authority ladder. Written Sep 27; 37 tests pass; Claude CLI, Jev and Astra verified live. Untested on the physical robot until Sep 30. Deck . Operation No human operation of the robot. Keyframes are taught by the vision model (LLM-servo); a person only answers questions in the viewer. Decided Sep 27. Servo loop verified against the simulator with the real model. Trays Fixed nests on the table: printed locating plate per cress planter with an AprilTag recess; printed light paddle and bottle rest. Parts generated for the M5C; unprinted. Actual planter meshes; conceptual table/robot placement. Bottle spout is a placeholder. Height, reach and structural capacity are untested. The next three useful actions Print on the M5C : the cress planter (6 pieces), two nest plates, the light paddle and the bottle rest. About one day of printing. Flash the ESP32 firmware and run farm sim --auto-answer on the Mac to see the whole program and the viewer before the robot arrives. September 30: assemble, farm devices → farm calibrate → farm check → farm teach-all → empty-bottle farm once . Build order . Removed from V0: electric watering pump, external reservoir, hoses/float switches, scale hardware, separate overhead camera and leak pads. The requested silicone mat, adhesive rubber sheets, plant labels and measuring syringes remain out. Use household measuring materials. This handbook resolves newer decisions over the original deck/redline. “Selected”, “printed”, “connected” and “validated” mean different things; every unresolved fit is listed where it matters. Last consolidated September 26, 2026.

title: Step-by-step guide
text: Do this next. Every step from an empty Mac to a robot that waters cress on its own: what to do, why, the exact commands, what you need, how long it takes, and a box to tick. Progress stays in this browser. 0 / 26 done Jump to next step Show all The whole journey 0 · Set up the Mac 2 h 1 · Print 1–4 days 2 · Electronics 2 h 3 · Assemble 4 h 4 · Bring-up 2 h 5 · Station 2 h 6 · Teach 1 h 7 · Water 2 h 8 · Run daily 9 · Hand over 2 h Phases 0–2 happen before the robot exists (in NY or on arrival). Phases 3–9 start September 30 in Japan. Phase 1 runs in the background: start the printer first, then do everything else while it prints. Estimated hands-on time is about two working days plus printing. Print first; everything else can overlap. 0 · Set up the Mac (do this today, anywhere) done Get the code and the tools ≈ 20 min Everything runs from one folder on the Mac. uv makes the Python environment in seconds; the tests prove the install before any hardware is involved. Install uv and Python 3.12 ( brew install uv python@3.12 ). Clone the repo and create the environment: git clone https://github.com/RonTuretzky/xlerobot-farm.git cd xlerobot-farm/software uv venv --python 3.12 .venv && . .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -e . python -m pytest -q # expect: 47 passed Run the whole program on fakes and open the viewer: farm sim --auto-answer # in a browser: http://localhost:8765 You should see two POURED cycles and the viewer with frames, questions and the STOP button. You need MacBook (the Neo) internet Links Software README uv install Done when pytest passed and farm sim showed two POURED cycles Watch out If pytest cannot import lerobot, the venv is not active: run . .venv/bin/activate first. done Log in to the model backends ≈ 15 min Vision (looking at trays, teaching poses) runs on your Claude subscription through the claude command line. Jev and Astra run through OpenRouter. Install and log in to Claude Code: quickstart , then run claude once and complete /login . Test headless: claude -p "reply with the JSON {\"ok\": true}" --output-format json Rotate the OpenRouter key (it was pasted in chat) at openrouter.ai/settings/keys , put a small credit limit on it, then: cp .env.example .env # edit .env: OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-… Check both from the farm: farm review -p sim # Astra proposal from the simulator’s evidence (uses OpenRouter) You need Claude subscription OpenRouter account with a few dollars Links OpenRouter keys Claude Code quickstart Done when claude -p returned JSON and farm review printed a proposal Watch out The profile caps OpenRouter spend at $5/day ( llm.max_cost_usd_per_day ); when hit, the robot refuses to pour rather than run blind. done Optional: questions on your phone (Telegram) ≈ 15 min The viewer works on the same Wi-Fi. Telegram lets the robot ask you anywhere: one message with buttons, your tap is the authorization record. Message @BotFather : /newbot , copy the token. Send your new bot any message, then open https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/getUpdates and copy your chat id. Add to .env : TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=123456:ABC… TELEGRAM_CHAT_IDS=987654321 From now on every question goes to the viewer and Telegram; the first answer wins. You need phone with Telegram Links BotFather Done when bot token and chat id in .env Watch out Only the chat ids listed can answer; anything else is ignored and logged. done Install a slicer for the AnkerMake M5C ≈ 15 min The M5C accepts G-code from AnkerMake Studio, PrusaSlicer or Cura. You only need one; AnkerMake Studio has the printer profile built in and sends jobs over Wi-Fi. Install AnkerMake Studio (or PrusaSlicer with the M5C profile) and pair the printer. Default profile for every part: 0.2 mm layers, 3 walls, 20 % infill, PLA 210–220 °C, bed 50–60 °C, no supports. Never run the Prusa MINI G-code from the modular-table download on the M5C: it is sliced for another machine. You need AnkerMake M5C on the same Wi-Fi 1.5 kg PLA (two spools) if you print the table, 0.5 kg without Links AnkerMake downloads M5C specs (Fabbaloo) Done when slicer installed and printer paired Watch out The 0.4 mm nozzle kit for the M5C is a different part from the K1 Max kit. 1 · Print the parts (start the printer, then keep going) done Print in this order ≈ 5 min Trays first (they gate the growing), then the nests (they gate the robot), then the small parts. The table is optional and long; start it last or skip it. Print queue on the AnkerMake M5C (hours, estimated; PLA grams) Cress planter (6 pieces) 10 h · 275 g Nest plate A 6.7 h · 93 g Nest plate B 6.7 h · 93 g Light paddle 0.9 h · 13 g Bottle rest 1.1 h · 16 g Tag tiles id1 + id2 0.2 h · 3 g Modular table (optional) 45 h · 1000 g Without the table: ≈ 26 h and ≈ 0.5 kg. With the table: ≈ 70 h and ≈ 1.5 kg (two spools). Planter time is the K1 Max slice (10h06m); the M5C is usually faster. Nest/paddle/rest are volume estimates at ~14 g/h. Table = creator’s 63 h on a Prusa MINI × ~0.7. Queue: cress planter (6 pieces) → nest A → nest B → paddle + bottle rest + tags on one plate → table (optional). Download: planter STLs · nest_cress.stl (print twice) · paddle · bottle rest · tag id1 · tag id2 . Tag tiles: pause at Z = 1.0 mm and switch to black filament for the raised cells, or colour the raised cells with a black marker afterwards. You need M5C PLA Links Parts README (assumptions to verify) Printing page Done when planter, two nests, paddle, rest and tags printed Watch out The square germination kit’s 220 mm tray does not fit the M5C; skip it or print it at 95 %. done Decide about the table (and what it costs) ≈ 10 min The robot needs the trays at a repeatable height within reach; it does not need a printed table. The chosen modular table works but is ~45 h of printing. Fast path: any stable surface at the right height (a box, a shelf, a cheap side table) with the nest plates screwed or taped to it. Zero print time. Printed path: Modular Table (100 % printed) , CC0. The creator’s table is 63 h / 909 g on a Prusa MINI; on the M5C expect ≈ 40–45 h and 0.9–1.2 kg for a top big enough for two nests (≈ 5 × 3 tiles). All parts fit the 220 mm bed. The 13 editable .3mf files are downloaded ( mirror ) and all fit the M5C bed; slice them yourself for the M5C. The other ZIP holds Prusa MINI G-code only: never send it to the M5C. Height: measure from the floor to the robot’s shoulders on the cart, subtract 5–10 cm: that is the tray-rim height you want. You need a decision Links Modular table files Done when table decided: surface chosen or table printing Watch out Pre-sliced per-part times from the download: 4 legs 7h48m (452 g), 8 connectors 3h19m (384 g), tops 1.4–2.3 h each — those are MINI times. done Check each print before trusting it ≈ 15 min A nest that is 1 mm tight or a rest that is 1 mm loose costs a whole teaching session later. Nest: the trough drops in and lifts out freely; the tag tile sits flush in its recess; the spout notch faces where the bottle will come from. Paddle: the BH1750 board fits its pocket; the handle grooves face the gripper. Bottle rest: your bottle drops in and stands vertical; if it wobbles, reprint with a smaller bore (edit make_parts.py ). Planter: rinse, fill the trough, leave it on paper for 30 min: no wet patch underneath. You need printed parts the real bottle BH1750 board Links Growing page: leak test Done when all fits checked, no leaks 2 · Electronics: the light sensor done Flash the ESP32 ≈ 30 min The ESP32 reads the light sensor and prints JSON over USB. Flashing is a one-time step with the Arduino IDE. Install the Arduino IDE , then add the ESP32 boards: Settings → Additional boards manager URLs → https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json → Boards Manager → install “esp32”. If the board does not show a serial port on macOS, install the CP210x or CH34x driver (check which chip your ELEGOO board has). Open software/firmware/esp32_light/esp32_light.ino , board “ESP32 Dev Module”, choose the port, Upload. Watch it: farm light-monitor # one line per second: lux, status, seq You need ELEGOO ESP32 USB data cable Arduino IDE Links Arduino-ESP32 install Firmware source Done when light-monitor shows lux changing when you cover the sensor Watch out A charge-only USB cable shows nothing. The cable from the cart must be a data cable. done Wire the BH1750 and mount it on the paddle ≈ 45 min Four wires. Get them right once and the sensor is a status-bearing reading for the rest of the project. ELEGOO ESP32 (ESP-WROOM-32) USB-C → powered hub (data cable!) Pins used: 3V3 → BH1750 VCC GND → BH1750 GND GPIO21 → BH1750 SDA GPIO22 → BH1750 SCL ADDR on the BH1750 left unconnected (= 0x23) BH1750 breakout VCC GND SCL SDA ADDR (leave open) 3V3 GND SDA SCL Paddle Board sits in the paddle pocket, sensor face UP. Four flexible wires run down the handle groove to the ESP32 on the cart. Check before power No short between 3V3 and GND (multimeter or careful look). The breakout accepts 3.3 V (most BH1750 boards do; read the silkscreen). Headers soldered if they arrived loose. Firmware prints one JSON line per reading at 115200 baud: {"seq":812,"t_ms":93410,"lux":412.5,"ok":true}. farm light-monitor shows it live. Solder the header pins onto the BH1750 if they came loose. Wire per the diagram (3V3, GND, GPIO21 → SDA, GPIO22 → SCL). Use the flexible 22 AWG wire; leave a service loop at the wrist. Screw the board into the paddle pocket, sensor face up; route the cable down the handle groove. Confirm again with farm light-monitor : cover / uncover the paddle. You need BH1750 flexible wire soldering iron (buy in Japan) printed paddle Links Hardware page BH1750 datasheet Done when paddle wired, readings valid while the cable is flexed Watch out Lux is not PPFD; the number is for comparing days, never for deciding water. 3 · Assemble the robot (Sep 30) done Assemble the robot ≈ 240 min The WowRobo two-wheel Combo arrives mostly assembled. Follow the vendor video for brackets and screws; our assembly page tracks integration checkpoints. Work through assembly steps 1–4 (lay out, cart + drive base, arms + head, cabling) with the WowRobo 0.4.0 (two-wheel) assembly video . First confirm the kit: two large drive wheels + casters = 0.4.0 (this video); three omni wheels = 0.3.0 ( older video ), and tell me, because the software profile assumes the two-wheel motor map. Power: use the two supplied 12 V/8 A wall adapters; check the labels accept 100 V (Japan). Battery stays out. Plug into the powered hub: 2 motor boards, 3 cameras, ESP32. Hub → Mac USB-3 port. Mac on its charger. You need WowRobo kit IKEA cart powered hub hex keys multimeter (borrowed) Links Assembly guide WowRobo 0.4.0 assembly video Older 0.3.0 video (three-wheel) Two-wheel reference Done when robot assembled, all USB devices on the hub, motors powered from wall adapters Watch out Never change a motor plug with motor power on. done Give the loose servos their IDs (the “FD” step in the video) ≈ 20 min At the start of the vendor video they use Feetech’s Windows program “FD” to type an ID into each loose servo. Every servo on a chain needs a unique ID: the arms come numbered 1–6, the two head servos must be 7 and 8, the two wheel servos 9 and 10. On the Mac the farm command does the same thing through the same motor board. Do this before the servos are mounted and chained. Plug ONE motor board into the Mac (USB) and its 12 V supply, and connect exactly ONE loose servo to it. Run the command for that servo, press ENTER when prompted, then label the servo with its number: cd software && . .venv/bin/activate farm set-motor-id --name head_motor_1 # → ID 7 farm set-motor-id --name head_motor_2 # → ID 8 farm set-motor-id --name base_left_wheel # → ID 9 farm set-motor-id --name base_right_wheel # → ID 10 Swap the servo between commands: only one servo on the board each time. If a servo already reports the right ID (some kits ship pre-numbered), the command simply confirms it. Later, farm devices --probe must show IDs 1–8 on one board (left arm + head) and 1–6, 9, 10 on the other (right arm + wheels). You need one motor board + its 12 V supply the four loose servos (2 head, 2 wheel) a marker for labels Links Vendor video (0.4.0), first minutes LeRobot: configure motors Done when four servos labelled 7, 8, 9, 10 Watch out Two servos with the same ID on one chain both go silent. Never set IDs with more than one servo connected. 4 · Bring the robot up on the Mac done Find the ports and cameras ≈ 15 min The profile must name the two motor buses and the three cameras by identity. The probe pings each bus and snapshots each camera so you do not guess. MacBook Neo Runs everything. No Raspberry Pi. Python · LeRobot · our farm code RSHTECH 7-port hub Own 5 V adapter. Carries USB data only. Never powers motors. USB-C · USB 3 Motor board A → bus 1 Left arm: 6 × STS3215 servos, IDs 1–6 Head pan / tilt: IDs 7–8 USB serial on the Mac: /dev/tty.usbmodem… 12 V / 8 A wall supply (separate) Motor board B → bus 2 Right arm: 6 × STS3215 servos, IDs 1–6 Drive wheels: IDs 9–10 (disabled in V0) USB serial on the Mac: /dev/tty.usbmodem… 12 V / 8 A wall supply (separate) Three USB cameras head · left wrist · right wrist OpenCV / AVFoundation, 640×480 @ 30 fps ELEGOO ESP32 (one of three) USB serial → JSON lines to the Mac I²C: BH1750 light sensor on the paddle BH1750 light paddle Gripped tool. 4 wires: 3V3, GND, SDA (GPIO21), SCL (GPIO22). Optional SHT31 air sensor On the body, not the arm. Same I²C bus. Moisture probe + relay Deferred for paper trays. Not wired. Bottle · trays · table No electronics. Known only through cameras and taught positions. Anker C300 (in hand) + wheels Owned, not wired: wall power and parked base for the whole trip. 12 V comes from its car outlet via a fused harness, not USB-C. Two facts shape the code: Everything is a USB device on one Mac. Motion is 14 servo positions; sensing is 3 images + 1 lux number. That is the whole interface. cd software && . .venv/bin/activate farm devices --probe The probe reports which port answers motor IDs 1–8 (bus 1: left arm + head) and which answers 9–10 (bus 2: right arm + wheels). Snapshots land in data/devices/ ; open them and decide which index is head, left wrist, right wrist. Edit profiles/paper-tray-v0.yaml : robot.port1 , robot.port2 , and index_or_path for each camera. You need assembled robot Links Profile file Done when profile has both ports and three camera indices Watch out macOS asks for camera permission the first time; allow it for Terminal. done Calibrate the joints once ≈ 20 min LeRobot needs each servo’s range once. This is the one setup step where a person moves the arms by hand — it is not operation. farm calibrate Follow the prompts: move the left arm + head to mid-range, ENTER; sweep every joint through its full range, ENTER; same for the right arm. The file lands in ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/robots/xlerobot_2wheels/ ; back it up. You need both arms supported motor power on Links LeRobot calibration docs Done when calibration file saved Watch out If a joint is skipped the model will later push it toward an impossible target and the safety clamp will stop everything. done Prove every device with one command ≈ 10 min Before any motion the program connects everything and asks the vision model to confirm which camera is which. A swapped camera is caught here, not over a tray. farm check Expect: problems: none , joints OK, health OK, three cameras OK, light OK, views: {"status": "OK", …} . If views says INVALID, two camera indices are swapped: fix the profile and re-run. Done when farm check is all OK Watch out Startup also marks any action that was ATTEMPTED before a crash as UNKNOWN and asks you to reconcile it in the viewer. 5 · Build the station done Lay out the station ≈ 60 min The program assumes nothing moves: trays in nests, bottle in its rest, paddle in its rest, cart parked. Everything the model teaches is relative to this layout. table (any stable surface at the right height) robot cart (parked) left arm right arm head cam comfortable reach ≈ 15–30 cm from each shoulder nest A · tray A nest B · tray B bottle rest (right side) paddle rest (left side) Heights Tray rim about 5–10 cm below the arm shoulders; the spout must clear the rim with the bottle upright. Measure before printing table legs. Nothing moves Nests screwed or taped down. Rests taped. Cart brakes on. If anything shifts, re-run farm teach-all. Light Bright, even, no direct sun on the cameras. A lamp behind the head camera is fine. Place the surface so the tray rims are 5–10 cm below the arm shoulders and 15–30 cm in front of them (see diagram). Screw or tape both nest plates down; drop a tag tile in each recess; set the cress planter into nest B (and A when you have two). Bottle rest on the right side within the right arm’s reach; paddle rest on the left. Tape them. Cart brakes on. Fill the bottle only half for the first days. A spout that pours a thin stream matters more than the bottle: the Nalgene needs a fitted spout or use a small squeeze bottle. You need nests, rests, tags planter with paper and water bottle with a spout tape / screws Links Growing page Prints page: nests Done when nothing on the station can move; bottle and paddle in their rests Watch out Direct sunlight on the wrist camera makes every judgement UNKNOWN. Shade the station. done Sow the first tray ≈ 20 min Cress on household paper: germinates in 2–4 days, so the robot has something to look at within the trip. Follow the setup steps : leak test, wick contact, sow a small even patch, keep an unseeded paper edge visible near the refill opening (the model judges wetness there). Log it in the notebook . You need cress seed (buy locally) kitchen paper water Done when tray sown, paper edge visible Watch out Do not carry seed or soil through customs; buy locally. 6 · Let the model teach the robot done Let the model teach every pose ≈ 60 min Nobody drives the arm. For each needed pose the vision model looks through the wrist and head cameras, moves in small clamped steps and saves the joints as a keyframe when the goal is visibly met. farm devices --probe ports + camera snapshots edit profile ports, camera indices farm calibrate one-time joint ranges farm check model confirms cameras farm teach-all model teaches poses farm once (empty) rehearsal, no water farm cup-test measure a pour farm once --tray B first real cycle farm run --every 3600 hourly, viewer + Telegram Orange = a person does something physical or types a value (setup). Blue = the program and the model do it. farm teach-all Watch the viewer (and stand near the STOP button). Each pose prints OK or FAILED with the model’s reason and cost. Poses learned: bottle rest above/grip, bottle upright, paddle rest above/grip, and per tray: look, pour, measure. Redo a single pose: farm teach --arm right --goal "spout 3 cm above the refill opening of tray B" --save pour_B You need station laid out bottle and paddle in rests Links LLM-servo source Done when teach-all reports failed: none Watch out If the model aborts with “target not visible”, fix the lighting or the head pose first; it is telling the truth. 7 · Water for the first time done Rehearse with an empty bottle ≈ 20 min The first full cycle must be dry: it proves pick, approach, tilt, upright and park without a drop of water. IDLE IDENTIFY INSPECT MEASURE LIGHT DECIDE PICK BOTTLE APPROACH POUR RETURN UPRIGHT VERIFY PARK evidence + deadline on every arrow rules → Jev → person · no “yes” → PARK, no water PAUSED (reason, evidence) Any check fails, any deadline passes, any adapter goes INVALID or STALE. Motors stop; bottle is returned upright first if it is held. UNKNOWN DELIVERY Crash or lost acknowledgement between POUR and VERIFY. Stays UNKNOWN until a person reconciles. Automatic retry is not an option. Human review Re-inspect, confirm physically, authorize, resolve, or take over. Only a person leaves PAUSED. Deadlines (profile): identify 10 s · inspect 20 s · measure 15 s · decide/ask 10 min · pick 30 s · pour ≤ 4 s tilt · verify 20 s · park 30 s. Implemented in farm/cycle/. Empty the bottle. Run: farm once --tray B The viewer asks “Authorize one pour?” — type your name, press authorize one pour . Watch the arm pick, approach, tilt, return upright, verify, park. Repeat until it is boring. Ten clean runs is the gate. Done when 10 clean empty-bottle cycles Watch out Press STOP in the viewer if anything looks wrong; motors hold instantly and only a named person can clear it. done Measure a real pour into a cup ≈ 15 min A tilt for N seconds is not a volume until you measure it. The cup test records the millilitres so every later pour is a known dose. farm cup-test --tilt 25 --seconds 1.5 --who yourname Hold a kitchen measure under the spout when prompted, read the millilitres, type them. Repeat with a fuller bottle; the last measurement is the calibration. You need kitchen measuring cup half-full bottle Done when pour calibration saved (data/pour_calibration.yaml) Watch out Aim for 20–30 mL per pour: enough to wet the reserve, never enough to flood the paper. done The first real cycle ≈ 20 min Now water goes into the tray. Rules, Jev and you all have to agree. localhost:8765 · farm viewer · tray B · cycle 0042 latest wrist frame age 0.6 s · right_wrist PAUSED reason: spill = UNKNOWN after pour (area under the rim not visible from right_wrist) last verified: RETURN_UPRIGHT ✓ 12:04:31 · fill ~40 mL (human, 11:58) evidence: obs 9124 · action 771 · decision rule:spill_gate Eligible next steps Re-inspect from head camera I looked: no spill, paper wet I looked: spill — cleaned, resolved Caretaker takes over this tray Retry pour — not offered while delivery is UNKNOWN Every press → intervention record: who, when, what was checked. Shadow (later): Jev suggested inspect_water 0.71 — logged, not acted on. Local network only. Not a safety device — stop rules live in the controller. farm once --tray B Authorize in the viewer. After the pour the model verifies: water visible / paper edge damp / spill CLEAR. If it cannot see the rim, the cycle pauses with delivery UNKNOWN and asks you to look. Open the cycle record in the viewer: every observation, decision and action with its status. Done when first POURED cycle with a VERIFIED pour Watch out A pour that ends UNKNOWN blocks every later cycle until you reconcile it. That is by design. 8 · Run it every day done Run hourly ≈ 5 min The care loop runs on a schedule, rests the arms between cycles (torque off so servos cool), and reconnects if a USB device hiccups. farm run --every 3600 Viewer: http://<mac-ip>:8765 from your phone on the same Wi-Fi (or Telegram). Leave the Mac on its charger with sleep disabled. Done when farm run has completed a day of cycles Watch out Keep the Mac awake: System Settings → Battery → prevent sleep on power, or run caffeinate -i farm run --every 3600 . done Let Jev earn authority ≈ 5 min Jev starts in shadow. After ten cycles where its route agreed with the rules and with you, it is promoted to route; after ten more agreeing pour decisions, to approve — it then authorizes routine pours and just notifies you. 1 · shadow Jev answers, is recorded, decides nothing. You authorize every pour in the viewer. earned 2 · route Jev’s “reinspect / pause” routes are honoured. You still authorize pours. earned 3 · approve Jev authorizes routine pours (p ≥ 0.85) when rules pass. You are notified. Promotion is automatic after jev_shadow_cycles agreeing cycles (profile: 10). A spill at reconciliation demotes. Any named person can set the level in the viewer. Nothing to do: promotion is automatic and recorded as events. Watch the Authority panel in the viewer. Demote at any time with the buttons; a spill at reconciliation demotes automatically. Links Deck: Jev and Astra Done when Jev reached route done Daily: Astra review, proposals, backup ≈ 10 min Once a day Astra reads the evidence and proposes one change. You accept or reject in the viewer. The database is backed up every day. farm review farm backup Open proposals appear in the viewer. authority.astra: apply-safe in the profile lets bounded numeric changes apply themselves. Done when first proposal reviewed and a backup exists done Turn the robot’s own runs into a learned pour (v2) ≈ 90 min Keyframes replay one pose; a learned policy re-aligns the grasp and spout from the cameras when the bottle sits slightly differently. The training data is the robot’s own successful runs — nobody demonstrates. Record while running (each cycle becomes an episode with 30 fps frames + joint targets): farm run --every 3600 --record # writes data/dataset (LeRobotDataset v3, .pos joint names, 3 cameras) Target 60–100 saved episodes (30–50 per tray); failed cycles are discarded automatically. Train locally (ACT, Apple-silicon GPU) or on a rented GPU (SmolVLA base, pretrained on SO-100/101 data): python -m farm.learning.train --policy act --dataset-root data/dataset --steps 20000 --device mps # or: python -m farm.learning.train --policy smolvla --dataset-root data/dataset --steps 20000 --job-target a10g-small Evaluate offline against held-out episodes, then run the checkpoint as a skill on the simulator and, with the STOP button in reach, on the robot: python -m farm.learning.evaluate --checkpoint data-train/act_farm/checkpoints/last/pretrained_model --dataset-root data/dataset farm policy-test --checkpoint data-train/act_farm/checkpoints/last/pretrained_model # simulator farm policy-test --checkpoint … --real --steps 100 # robot, clamped, e-stop ready Only when it beats the keyframe skill on held-out episodes: set policy.enabled: true (shadow first) in the profile. You need 60–100 recorded episodes Mac (ACT) or a rented GPU (SmolVLA) Links Research: data and policies that exist Best same-arm pour data (100 ep) SmolVLA base Done when a checkpoint exists and farm policy-test ran it on the simulator Watch out Already done once as a pipeline check (Sep 27): ACT on 35 public SO-101 bottle-pour episodes, 5000 steps in ~70 min on the Mac, loss 3.3 → 0.42, checkpoint drove the simulator. That checkpoint is a motion prior for someone else’s table: the last 10–20 cm to our tray only comes from our own episodes. An offline error is not a success rate. 9 · Grow, review, hand over done Daily plant checks ≈ 10 min The robot inspects and waters; a person still looks at the crop once a day and writes two lines. The photos are in the viewer. Follow the daily plan : paper evenly damp, no puddles, cover off once shoots stand, bright light. Log observations in the notebook; note every manual top-up as an intervention. title: The whole journey
text: The whole journey 0 · Set up the Mac 2 h 1 · Print 1–4 days 2 · Electronics 2 h 3 · Assemble 4 h 4 · Bring-up 2 h 5 · Station 2 h 6 · Teach 1 h 7 · Water 2 h 8 · Run daily 9 · Hand over 2 h Phases 0–2 happen before the robot exists (in NY or on arrival). Phases 3–9 start September 30 in Japan. Phase 1 runs in the background: start the printer first, then do everything else while it prints. Estimated hands-on time is about two working days plus printing. Print first; everything else can overlap.

title: 0 · Set up the Mac (do this today, anywhere)
text: 0 · Set up the Mac (do this today, anywhere) done Get the code and the tools ≈ 20 min Everything runs from one folder on the Mac. uv makes the Python environment in seconds; the tests prove the install before any hardware is involved. Install uv and Python 3.12 ( brew install uv python@3.12 ). Clone the repo and create the environment: git clone https://github.com/RonTuretzky/xlerobot-farm.git cd xlerobot-farm/software uv venv --python 3.12 .venv && . .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -e . python -m pytest -q # expect: 47 passed Run the whole program on fakes and open the viewer: farm sim --auto-answer # in a browser: http://localhost:8765 You should see two POURED cycles and the viewer with frames, questions and the STOP button. You need MacBook (the Neo) internet Links Software README uv install Done when pytest passed and farm sim showed two POURED cycles Watch out If pytest cannot import lerobot, the venv is not active: run . .venv/bin/activate first. done Log in to the model backends ≈ 15 min Vision (looking at trays, teaching poses) runs on your Claude subscription through the claude command line. Jev and Astra run through OpenRouter. Install and log in to Claude Code: quickstart , then run claude once and complete /login . Test headless: claude -p "reply with the JSON {\"ok\": true}" --output-format json Rotate the OpenRouter key (it was pasted in chat) at openrouter.ai/settings/keys , put a small credit limit on it, then: cp .env.example .env # edit .env: OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-… Check both from the farm: farm review -p sim # Astra proposal from the simulator’s evidence (uses OpenRouter) You need Claude subscription OpenRouter account with a few dollars Links OpenRouter keys Claude Code quickstart Done when claude -p returned JSON and farm review printed a proposal Watch out The profile caps OpenRouter spend at $5/day ( llm.max_cost_usd_per_day ); when hit, the robot refuses to pour rather than run blind. done Optional: questions on your phone (Telegram) ≈ 15 min The viewer works on the same Wi-Fi. Telegram lets the robot ask you anywhere: one message with buttons, your tap is the authorization record. Message @BotFather : /newbot , copy the token. Send your new bot any message, then open https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/getUpdates and copy your chat id. Add to .env : TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=123456:ABC… TELEGRAM_CHAT_IDS=987654321 From now on every question goes to the viewer and Telegram; the first answer wins. You need phone with Telegram Links BotFather Done when bot token and chat id in .env Watch out Only the chat ids listed can answer; anything else is ignored and logged. done Install a slicer for the AnkerMake M5C ≈ 15 min The M5C accepts G-code from AnkerMake Studio, PrusaSlicer or Cura. You only need one; AnkerMake Studio has the printer profile built in and sends jobs over Wi-Fi. Install AnkerMake Studio (or PrusaSlicer with the M5C profile) and pair the printer. Default profile for every part: 0.2 mm layers, 3 walls, 20 % infill, PLA 210–220 °C, bed 50–60 °C, no supports. Never run the Prusa MINI G-code from the modular-table download on the M5C: it is sliced for another machine. You need AnkerMake M5C on the same Wi-Fi 1.5 kg PLA (two spools) if you print the table, 0.5 kg without Links AnkerMake downloads M5C specs (Fabbaloo) Done when slicer installed and printer paired Watch out The 0.4 mm nozzle kit for the M5C is a different part from the K1 Max kit.

title: 1 · Print the parts (start the printer, then keep going)
text: 1 · Print the parts (start the printer, then keep going) done Print in this order ≈ 5 min Trays first (they gate the growing), then the nests (they gate the robot), then the small parts. The table is optional and long; start it last or skip it. Print queue on the AnkerMake M5C (hours, estimated; PLA grams) Cress planter (6 pieces) 10 h · 275 g Nest plate A 6.7 h · 93 g Nest plate B 6.7 h · 93 g Light paddle 0.9 h · 13 g Bottle rest 1.1 h · 16 g Tag tiles id1 + id2 0.2 h · 3 g Modular table (optional) 45 h · 1000 g Without the table: ≈ 26 h and ≈ 0.5 kg. With the table: ≈ 70 h and ≈ 1.5 kg (two spools). Planter time is the K1 Max slice (10h06m); the M5C is usually faster. Nest/paddle/rest are volume estimates at ~14 g/h. Table = creator’s 63 h on a Prusa MINI × ~0.7. Queue: cress planter (6 pieces) → nest A → nest B → paddle + bottle rest + tags on one plate → table (optional). Download: planter STLs · nest_cress.stl (print twice) · paddle · bottle rest · tag id1 · tag id2 . Tag tiles: pause at Z = 1.0 mm and switch to black filament for the raised cells, or colour the raised cells with a black marker afterwards. You need M5C PLA Links Parts README (assumptions to verify) Printing page Done when planter, two nests, paddle, rest and tags printed Watch out The square germination kit’s 220 mm tray does not fit the M5C; skip it or print it at 95 %. done Decide about the table (and what it costs) ≈ 10 min The robot needs the trays at a repeatable height within reach; it does not need a printed table. The chosen modular table works but is ~45 h of printing. Fast path: any stable surface at the right height (a box, a shelf, a cheap side table) with the nest plates screwed or taped to it. Zero print time. Printed path: Modular Table (100 % printed) , CC0. The creator’s table is 63 h / 909 g on a Prusa MINI; on the M5C expect ≈ 40–45 h and 0.9–1.2 kg for a top big enough for two nests (≈ 5 × 3 tiles). All parts fit the 220 mm bed. The 13 editable .3mf files are downloaded ( mirror ) and all fit the M5C bed; slice them yourself for the M5C. The other ZIP holds Prusa MINI G-code only: never send it to the M5C. Height: measure from the floor to the robot’s shoulders on the cart, subtract 5–10 cm: that is the tray-rim height you want. You need a decision Links Modular table files Done when table decided: surface chosen or table printing Watch out Pre-sliced per-part times from the download: 4 legs 7h48m (452 g), 8 connectors 3h19m (384 g), tops 1.4–2.3 h each — those are MINI times. done Check each print before trusting it ≈ 15 min A nest that is 1 mm tight or a rest that is 1 mm loose costs a whole teaching session later. Nest: the trough drops in and lifts out freely; the tag tile sits flush in its recess; the spout notch faces where the bottle will come from. Paddle: the BH1750 board fits its pocket; the handle grooves face the gripper. Bottle rest: your bottle drops in and stands vertical; if it wobbles, reprint with a smaller bore (edit make_parts.py ). Planter: rinse, fill the trough, leave it on paper for 30 min: no wet patch underneath. You need printed parts the real bottle BH1750 board Links Growing page: leak test Done when all fits checked, no leaks

title: 2 · Electronics: the light sensor
text: 2 · Electronics: the light sensor done Flash the ESP32 ≈ 30 min The ESP32 reads the light sensor and prints JSON over USB. Flashing is a one-time step with the Arduino IDE. Install the Arduino IDE , then add the ESP32 boards: Settings → Additional boards manager URLs → https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json → Boards Manager → install “esp32”. If the board does not show a serial port on macOS, install the CP210x or CH34x driver (check which chip your ELEGOO board has). Open software/firmware/esp32_light/esp32_light.ino , board “ESP32 Dev Module”, choose the port, Upload. Watch it: farm light-monitor # one line per second: lux, status, seq You need ELEGOO ESP32 USB data cable Arduino IDE Links Arduino-ESP32 install Firmware source Done when light-monitor shows lux changing when you cover the sensor Watch out A charge-only USB cable shows nothing. The cable from the cart must be a data cable. done Wire the BH1750 and mount it on the paddle ≈ 45 min Four wires. Get them right once and the sensor is a status-bearing reading for the rest of the project. ELEGOO ESP32 (ESP-WROOM-32) USB-C → powered hub (data cable!) Pins used: 3V3 → BH1750 VCC GND → BH1750 GND GPIO21 → BH1750 SDA GPIO22 → BH1750 SCL ADDR on the BH1750 left unconnected (= 0x23) BH1750 breakout VCC GND SCL SDA ADDR (leave open) 3V3 GND SDA SCL Paddle Board sits in the paddle pocket, sensor face UP. Four flexible wires run down the handle groove to the ESP32 on the cart. Check before power No short between 3V3 and GND (multimeter or careful look). The breakout accepts 3.3 V (most BH1750 boards do; read the silkscreen). Headers soldered if they arrived loose. Firmware prints one JSON line per reading at 115200 baud: {"seq":812,"t_ms":93410,"lux":412.5,"ok":true}. farm light-monitor shows it live. Solder the header pins onto the BH1750 if they came loose. Wire per the diagram (3V3, GND, GPIO21 → SDA, GPIO22 → SCL). Use the flexible 22 AWG wire; leave a service loop at the wrist. Screw the board into the paddle pocket, sensor face up; route the cable down the handle groove. Confirm again with farm light-monitor : cover / uncover the paddle. You need BH1750 flexible wire soldering iron (buy in Japan) printed paddle Links Hardware page BH1750 datasheet Done when paddle wired, readings valid while the cable is flexed Watch out Lux is not PPFD; the number is for comparing days, never for deciding water.

title: 3 · Assemble the robot (Sep 30)
text: 3 · Assemble the robot (Sep 30) done Assemble the robot ≈ 240 min The WowRobo two-wheel Combo arrives mostly assembled. Follow the vendor video for brackets and screws; our assembly page tracks integration checkpoints. Work through assembly steps 1–4 (lay out, cart + drive base, arms + head, cabling) with the WowRobo 0.4.0 (two-wheel) assembly video . First confirm the kit: two large drive wheels + casters = 0.4.0 (this video); three omni wheels = 0.3.0 ( older video ), and tell me, because the software profile assumes the two-wheel motor map. Power: use the two supplied 12 V/8 A wall adapters; check the labels accept 100 V (Japan). Battery stays out. Plug into the powered hub: 2 motor boards, 3 cameras, ESP32. Hub → Mac USB-3 port. Mac on its charger. You need WowRobo kit IKEA cart powered hub hex keys multimeter (borrowed) Links Assembly guide WowRobo 0.4.0 assembly video Older 0.3.0 video (three-wheel) Two-wheel reference Done when robot assembled, all USB devices on the hub, motors powered from wall adapters Watch out Never change a motor plug with motor power on. done Give the loose servos their IDs (the “FD” step in the video) ≈ 20 min At the start of the vendor video they use Feetech’s Windows program “FD” to type an ID into each loose servo. Every servo on a chain needs a unique ID: the arms come numbered 1–6, the two head servos must be 7 and 8, the two wheel servos 9 and 10. On the Mac the farm command does the same thing through the same motor board. Do this before the servos are mounted and chained. Plug ONE motor board into the Mac (USB) and its 12 V supply, and connect exactly ONE loose servo to it. Run the command for that servo, press ENTER when prompted, then label the servo with its number: cd software && . .venv/bin/activate farm set-motor-id --name head_motor_1 # → ID 7 farm set-motor-id --name head_motor_2 # → ID 8 farm set-motor-id --name base_left_wheel # → ID 9 farm set-motor-id --name base_right_wheel # → ID 10 Swap the servo between commands: only one servo on the board each time. If a servo already reports the right ID (some kits ship pre-numbered), the command simply confirms it. Later, farm devices --probe must show IDs 1–8 on one board (left arm + head) and 1–6, 9, 10 on the other (right arm + wheels). You need one motor board + its 12 V supply the four loose servos (2 head, 2 wheel) a marker for labels Links Vendor video (0.4.0), first minutes LeRobot: configure motors Done when four servos labelled 7, 8, 9, 10 Watch out Two servos with the same ID on one chain both go silent. Never set IDs with more than one servo connected.

title: 4 · Bring the robot up on the Mac
text: 4 · Bring the robot up on the Mac done Find the ports and cameras ≈ 15 min The profile must name the two motor buses and the three cameras by identity. The probe pings each bus and snapshots each camera so you do not guess. MacBook Neo Runs everything. No Raspberry Pi. Python · LeRobot · our farm code RSHTECH 7-port hub Own 5 V adapter. Carries USB data only. Never powers motors. USB-C · USB 3 Motor board A → bus 1 Left arm: 6 × STS3215 servos, IDs 1–6 Head pan / tilt: IDs 7–8 USB serial on the Mac: /dev/tty.usbmodem… 12 V / 8 A wall supply (separate) Motor board B → bus 2 Right arm: 6 × STS3215 servos, IDs 1–6 Drive wheels: IDs 9–10 (disabled in V0) USB serial on the Mac: /dev/tty.usbmodem… 12 V / 8 A wall supply (separate) Three USB cameras head · left wrist · right wrist OpenCV / AVFoundation, 640×480 @ 30 fps ELEGOO ESP32 (one of three) USB serial → JSON lines to the Mac I²C: BH1750 light sensor on the paddle BH1750 light paddle Gripped tool. 4 wires: 3V3, GND, SDA (GPIO21), SCL (GPIO22). Optional SHT31 air sensor On the body, not the arm. Same I²C bus. Moisture probe + relay Deferred for paper trays. Not wired. Bottle · trays · table No electronics. Known only through cameras and taught positions. Anker C300 (in hand) + wheels Owned, not wired: wall power and parked base for the whole trip. 12 V comes from its car outlet via a fused harness, not USB-C. Two facts shape the code: Everything is a USB device on one Mac. Motion is 14 servo positions; sensing is 3 images + 1 lux number. That is the whole interface. cd software && . .venv/bin/activate farm devices --probe The probe reports which port answers motor IDs 1–8 (bus 1: left arm + head) and which answers 9–10 (bus 2: right arm + wheels). Snapshots land in data/devices/ ; open them and decide which index is head, left wrist, right wrist. Edit profiles/paper-tray-v0.yaml : robot.port1 , robot.port2 , and index_or_path for each camera. You need assembled robot Links Profile file Done when profile has both ports and three camera indices Watch out macOS asks for camera permission the first time; allow it for Terminal. done Calibrate the joints once ≈ 20 min LeRobot needs each servo’s range once. This is the one setup step where a person moves the arms by hand — it is not operation. farm calibrate Follow the prompts: move the left arm + head to mid-range, ENTER; sweep every joint through its full range, ENTER; same for the right arm. The file lands in ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/robots/xlerobot_2wheels/ ; back it up. You need both arms supported motor power on Links LeRobot calibration docs Done when calibration file saved Watch out If a joint is skipped the model will later push it toward an impossible target and the safety clamp will stop everything. done Prove every device with one command ≈ 10 min Before any motion the program connects everything and asks the vision model to confirm which camera is which. A swapped camera is caught here, not over a tray. farm check Expect: problems: none , joints OK, health OK, three cameras OK, light OK, views: {"status": "OK", …} . If views says INVALID, two camera indices are swapped: fix the profile and re-run. Done when farm check is all OK Watch out Startup also marks any action that was ATTEMPTED before a crash as UNKNOWN and asks you to reconcile it in the viewer.

title: 5 · Build the station
text: 5 · Build the station done Lay out the station ≈ 60 min The program assumes nothing moves: trays in nests, bottle in its rest, paddle in its rest, cart parked. Everything the model teaches is relative to this layout. table (any stable surface at the right height) robot cart (parked) left arm right arm head cam comfortable reach ≈ 15–30 cm from each shoulder nest A · tray A nest B · tray B bottle rest (right side) paddle rest (left side) Heights Tray rim about 5–10 cm below the arm shoulders; the spout must clear the rim with the bottle upright. Measure before printing table legs. Nothing moves Nests screwed or taped down. Rests taped. Cart brakes on. If anything shifts, re-run farm teach-all. Light Bright, even, no direct sun on the cameras. A lamp behind the head camera is fine. Place the surface so the tray rims are 5–10 cm below the arm shoulders and 15–30 cm in front of them (see diagram). Screw or tape both nest plates down; drop a tag tile in each recess; set the cress planter into nest B (and A when you have two). Bottle rest on the right side within the right arm’s reach; paddle rest on the left. Tape them. Cart brakes on. Fill the bottle only half for the first days. A spout that pours a thin stream matters more than the bottle: the Nalgene needs a fitted spout or use a small squeeze bottle. You need nests, rests, tags planter with paper and water bottle with a spout tape / screws Links Growing page Prints page: nests Done when nothing on the station can move; bottle and paddle in their rests Watch out Direct sunlight on the wrist camera makes every judgement UNKNOWN. Shade the station. done Sow the first tray ≈ 20 min Cress on household paper: germinates in 2–4 days, so the robot has something to look at within the trip. Follow the setup steps : leak test, wick contact, sow a small even patch, keep an unseeded paper edge visible near the refill opening (the model judges wetness there). Log it in the notebook . You need cress seed (buy locally) kitchen paper water Done when tray sown, paper edge visible Watch out Do not carry seed or soil through customs; buy locally.

title: 6 · Let the model teach the robot
text: 6 · Let the model teach the robot done Let the model teach every pose ≈ 60 min Nobody drives the arm. For each needed pose the vision model looks through the wrist and head cameras, moves in small clamped steps and saves the joints as a keyframe when the goal is visibly met. farm devices --probe ports + camera snapshots edit profile ports, camera indices farm calibrate one-time joint ranges farm check model confirms cameras farm teach-all model teaches poses farm once (empty) rehearsal, no water farm cup-test measure a pour farm once --tray B first real cycle farm run --every 3600 hourly, viewer + Telegram Orange = a person does something physical or types a value (setup). Blue = the program and the model do it. farm teach-all Watch the viewer (and stand near the STOP button). Each pose prints OK or FAILED with the model’s reason and cost. Poses learned: bottle rest above/grip, bottle upright, paddle rest above/grip, and per tray: look, pour, measure. Redo a single pose: farm teach --arm right --goal "spout 3 cm above the refill opening of tray B" --save pour_B You need station laid out bottle and paddle in rests Links LLM-servo source Done when teach-all reports failed: none Watch out If the model aborts with “target not visible”, fix the lighting or the head pose first; it is telling the truth.

title: 7 · Water for the first time
text: 7 · Water for the first time done Rehearse with an empty bottle ≈ 20 min The first full cycle must be dry: it proves pick, approach, tilt, upright and park without a drop of water. IDLE IDENTIFY INSPECT MEASURE LIGHT DECIDE PICK BOTTLE APPROACH POUR RETURN UPRIGHT VERIFY PARK evidence + deadline on every arrow rules → Jev → person · no “yes” → PARK, no water PAUSED (reason, evidence) Any check fails, any deadline passes, any adapter goes INVALID or STALE. Motors stop; bottle is returned upright first if it is held. UNKNOWN DELIVERY Crash or lost acknowledgement between POUR and VERIFY. Stays UNKNOWN until a person reconciles. Automatic retry is not an option. Human review Re-inspect, confirm physically, authorize, resolve, or take over. Only a person leaves PAUSED. Deadlines (profile): identify 10 s · inspect 20 s · measure 15 s · decide/ask 10 min · pick 30 s · pour ≤ 4 s tilt · verify 20 s · park 30 s. Implemented in farm/cycle/. Empty the bottle. Run: farm once --tray B The viewer asks “Authorize one pour?” — type your name, press authorize one pour . Watch the arm pick, approach, tilt, return upright, verify, park. Repeat until it is boring. Ten clean runs is the gate. Done when 10 clean empty-bottle cycles Watch out Press STOP in the viewer if anything looks wrong; motors hold instantly and only a named person can clear it. done Measure a real pour into a cup ≈ 15 min A tilt for N seconds is not a volume until you measure it. The cup test records the millilitres so every later pour is a known dose. farm cup-test --tilt 25 --seconds 1.5 --who yourname Hold a kitchen measure under the spout when prompted, read the millilitres, type them. Repeat with a fuller bottle; the last measurement is the calibration. You need kitchen measuring cup half-full bottle Done when pour calibration saved (data/pour_calibration.yaml) Watch out Aim for 20–30 mL per pour: enough to wet the reserve, never enough to flood the paper. done The first real cycle ≈ 20 min Now water goes into the tray. Rules, Jev and you all have to agree. localhost:8765 · farm viewer · tray B · cycle 0042 latest wrist frame age 0.6 s · right_wrist PAUSED reason: spill = UNKNOWN after pour (area under the rim not visible from right_wrist) last verified: RETURN_UPRIGHT ✓ 12:04:31 · fill ~40 mL (human, 11:58) evidence: obs 9124 · action 771 · decision rule:spill_gate Eligible next steps Re-inspect from head camera I looked: no spill, paper wet I looked: spill — cleaned, resolved Caretaker takes over this tray Retry pour — not offered while delivery is UNKNOWN Every press → intervention record: who, when, what was checked. Shadow (later): Jev suggested inspect_water 0.71 — logged, not acted on. Local network only. Not a safety device — stop rules live in the controller. farm once --tray B Authorize in the viewer. After the pour the model verifies: water visible / paper edge damp / spill CLEAR. If it cannot see the rim, the cycle pauses with delivery UNKNOWN and asks you to look. Open the cycle record in the viewer: every observation, decision and action with its status. Done when first POURED cycle with a VERIFIED pour Watch out A pour that ends UNKNOWN blocks every later cycle until you reconcile it. That is by design.

title: 8 · Run it every day
text: 8 · Run it every day done Run hourly ≈ 5 min The care loop runs on a schedule, rests the arms between cycles (torque off so servos cool), and reconnects if a USB device hiccups. farm run --every 3600 Viewer: http://<mac-ip>:8765 from your phone on the same Wi-Fi (or Telegram). Leave the Mac on its charger with sleep disabled. Done when farm run has completed a day of cycles Watch out Keep the Mac awake: System Settings → Battery → prevent sleep on power, or run caffeinate -i farm run --every 3600 . done Let Jev earn authority ≈ 5 min Jev starts in shadow. After ten cycles where its route agreed with the rules and with you, it is promoted to route; after ten more agreeing pour decisions, to approve — it then authorizes routine pours and just notifies you. 1 · shadow Jev answers, is recorded, decides nothing. You authorize every pour in the viewer. earned 2 · route Jev’s “reinspect / pause” routes are honoured. You still authorize pours. earned 3 · approve Jev authorizes routine pours (p ≥ 0.85) when rules pass. You are notified. Promotion is automatic after jev_shadow_cycles agreeing cycles (profile: 10). A spill at reconciliation demotes. Any named person can set the level in the viewer. Nothing to do: promotion is automatic and recorded as events. Watch the Authority panel in the viewer. Demote at any time with the buttons; a spill at reconciliation demotes automatically. Links Deck: Jev and Astra Done when Jev reached route done Daily: Astra review, proposals, backup ≈ 10 min Once a day Astra reads the evidence and proposes one change. You accept or reject in the viewer. The database is backed up every day. farm review farm backup Open proposals appear in the viewer. authority.astra: apply-safe in the profile lets bounded numeric changes apply themselves. Done when first proposal reviewed and a backup exists done Turn the robot’s own runs into a learned pour (v2) ≈ 90 min Keyframes replay one pose; a learned policy re-aligns the grasp and spout from the cameras when the bottle sits slightly differently. The training data is the robot’s own successful runs — nobody demonstrates. Record while running (each cycle becomes an episode with 30 fps frames + joint targets): farm run --every 3600 --record # writes data/dataset (LeRobotDataset v3, .pos joint names, 3 cameras) Target 60–100 saved episodes (30–50 per tray); failed cycles are discarded automatically. Train locally (ACT, Apple-silicon GPU) or on a rented GPU (SmolVLA base, pretrained on SO-100/101 data): python -m farm.learning.train --policy act --dataset-root data/dataset --steps 20000 --device mps # or: python -m farm.learning.train --policy smolvla --dataset-root data/dataset --steps 20000 --job-target a10g-small Evaluate offline against held-out episodes, then run the checkpoint as a skill on the simulator and, with the STOP button in reach, on the robot: python -m farm.learning.evaluate --checkpoint data-train/act_farm/checkpoints/last/pretrained_model --dataset-root data/dataset farm policy-test --checkpoint data-train/act_farm/checkpoints/last/pretrained_model # simulator farm policy-test --checkpoint … --real --steps 100 # robot, clamped, e-stop ready Only when it beats the keyframe skill on held-out episodes: set policy.enabled: true (shadow first) in the profile. You need 60–100 recorded episodes Mac (ACT) or a rented GPU (SmolVLA) Links Research: data and policies that exist Best same-arm pour data (100 ep) SmolVLA base Done when a checkpoint exists and farm policy-test ran it on the simulator Watch out Already done once as a pipeline check (Sep 27): ACT on 35 public SO-101 bottle-pour episodes, 5000 steps in ~70 min on the Mac, loss 3.3 → 0.42, checkpoint drove the simulator. That checkpoint is a motion prior for someone else’s table: the last 10–20 cm to our tray only comes from our own episodes. An offline error is not a success rate.

title: 9 · Grow, review, hand over
text: 9 · Grow, review, hand over done Daily plant checks ≈ 10 min The robot inspects and waters; a person still looks at the crop once a day and writes two lines. The photos are in the viewer. Follow the daily plan : paper evenly damp, no puddles, cover off once shoots stand, bright light. Log observations in the notebook; note every manual top-up as an intervention. Links Growing page Done when day 6: germination photographed done Hand over (Oct 9–10) ≈ 60 min The project is done when someone else can run it: restore a backup, resolve a staged pause, refill the bottle, and know where the records are. Export: farm backup ; copy data/ (SQLite + images + keyframes + calibration) somewhere safe. Stage a pause (cover the rim with a card during a cycle) and have the caretaker resolve it in the viewer. Write down: viewer URL, Telegram bot, STOP, the reconcile buttons, who to call. Links Deck: build order Done when another person resolved a staged exception

text: Readiness audit: everything the project needs Item Status Note Robot kit (WowRobo two-wheel Combo), cart, hub, battery ordered / owned Confirm the packing list on arrival; battery stays out of V0. Group the two arms and their motor controllers, two drive assemblies, head assembly, three cameras, bracket/fastener bags, two motor supplies and supplied USB/motor leads. Keep the original bags with their labels. Photograph motor and adapter labels. Confirm this is the two-wheel servo version and that each motor supply matches its controller and motors. An adapter fitting the socket is not sufficient. Set aside the farm sensors, growing parts and battery. Have a screwdriver/hex keys matching the supplied screws and a borrowed multimeter for electrical checks. Kit revision, voltage labels and all supplied part groups identified. Step 02 Assemble the IKEA cart and drive base On the bench: Cart, two drive modules, printed brackets, bearings, supplied screws and motor extensions. Assemble the cart to its own manual. Build and mount each drive module in the video’s orientation and screw order. Use the kit’s bearings, wheel hubs and fasteners; do not substitute the older three-wheel plate. Route supplied motor extensions upward with protected edges and slack. Keep wheels free of dangling leads. Do not cut cart mesh until the delivered bracket and cable route establish where an opening is needed. Base sits securely, wheels clear the structure, and no lead can enter a wheel. Step 03 Mount the arms and head On the bench: Assembled follower arms, top mounts/clamps, head pan/tilt parts, three camera mounts. Support each arm while fastening its mount to the top structure in the vendor orientation. Skip rebuilding an already assembled arm; check for loose joints and cracked prints. Assemble the head pan/tilt mechanism using the supplied hardware. Mount the head camera and each wrist camera if not already fitted. Leave the grippers empty. Place the intended plant surface beside the parked cart and check approximate reach without forcing any joint. The planter table is separate from the robot cart. Both arm bases and the head are secure; cameras have unobstructed views. Step 04 Finish robot cabling before power On the bench: Supplied motor harnesses, camera leads, motor-controller USB cables and cable retainers. Use the delivered wiring map to connect each motor chain to the correct controller, including head and drive extensions. Label the two controller USB leads so they cannot be confused later. Keep motor power disconnected while changing motor plugs. Match connector orientation and pin order; do not splice the farm wire into the motor chain. Retain camera and motor cables at fixed points, with service loops at moving joints. Check that wrist motion cannot pull a plug or stretch a cable. Robot wiring matches the delivered revision and all plugs are seated with power off. For unassembled arms, use the SO101 joint-by-joint instructions . Both XLeRobot arms are followers; a generic leader/follower tutorial does not make one of these a leader. 5–8 · Connect the Mac and prove basic motion USB carries control and camera data. Motor power is separate. Probe equipment shown in the broader render is optional for the paper-tray build. Step 05 Connect the powered hub and identify USB devices On the bench: RSHTECH RSH-ST07, its adapter and upstream cable, MacBook, robot USB leads. Connect the hub’s own supplied power adapter, then its upstream data cable to the Mac’s USB 3-capable port. Keep the Mac on its charger. Do not assume a downstream charging port is the hub’s upstream port. Plug in one motor controller at a time and record its serial-device name, then connect each camera and identify head, left wrist and right wrist by covering the lens briefly. Use the connection checklist below for port labels. Nothing on a USB cable alone powers the arm motors. Two controller identities and three camera identities recorded without guessing indices. Step 06 Install a matching robot software version On the bench: Mac, XLeRobot source and compatible LeRobot environment. Follow the XLeRobot installation guide and its compatible LeRobot revision; record both versions. Do not mix commands from old tutorials with a newly upgraded environment. Use the SO101 guide’s port-discovery tool to map the actual Mac serial ports. Configure those paths in the robot settings instead of Linux /dev/ttyACM names. Select the two-wheel configuration and its expected motor map. Check that the installed code supports the delivered base before commanding it. macOS support for individual serial tools is not proof that every full-robot demo works. Software versions, Mac ports, camera names and two-wheel profile recorded. Step 07 Power, identify and calibrate one arm at a time On the bench: Matched kit motor supply, empty supported arm, reachable power disconnect. Confirm adapter input accepts the local mains and output matches the motor labels. Use the supplied wall supplies for commissioning. Apply motor power last; disconnect it before changing motor wiring. Check the preconfigured motor IDs before changing them. If configuration is required, use the documented one-motor-at-a-time procedure; never rename a whole connected chain blindly. Calibrate each follower arm with a unique name. Follow the tool’s midpoint and range prompts with torque disabled as directed; support the arm and stay within mechanical limits. Save the resulting calibration files. Both arms report the expected motors and have separate saved calibrations. Step 08 Test cameras and small movements without water On the bench: Assembled robot, all USB devices, empty grippers and empty work area. Start a single-joint control example at conservative motion limits. Test direction and stopping on one arm, then the other, then the head. Keep base motion disabled during the first farm setup. Open the camera streams together at modest supported resolution/frame rate. Label the views and check for dropped frames while moving an arm; lower bandwidth if necessary. Test the configured stop action with empty grippers and supported arms. Once controls are dependable, rehearse reaching an empty tray and returning to rest. Small motions, camera coverage and stopping work together without cable pulls or USB resets. References: XLeRobot installation , SO101 port setup/calibration , single-arm examples . These are setup instructions; no robot software has been installed or tested by this website. 9–11 · Add just one light sensor Use one BH1750, with its sensing face upward. The ESP32 stays on the dry robot body. The gripper holds the paddle only while taking a reading. Step 09 Wire a short light-sensor circuit on the bench On the bench: One ELEGOO ESP32, one BH1750, USB data cable, breadboard and jumper wires. With USB unplugged, read the labels on both boards. Fit headers only if needed; solder loose headers into their plated holes. Already installed headers require no soldering. For a verified ESP-WROOM-32 board, our proposed assignment is BH1750 VCC to ESP32 3V3, GND to GND, SDA to GPIO21 and SCL to GPIO22. Match by GPIO label, not physical pin number. Confirm the actual breakout accepts 3.3V and its bus pull-ups do not exceed 3.3V. Check for shorts, then power the ESP32 only through its USB data cable from the hub. Configure firmware to the same SDA/SCL pins, detect the sensor and log lux over serial. Cover/uncover the sensor and confirm the reading changes. Light readings reach the Mac and change reliably when shaded. Step 10 Fit the printed paddle and flexible harness On the bench: Light paddle prototype, BH1750, flexible wire, retained connector and dry ESP32 enclosure. Dry-fit the actual board to the paddle; the prototype is not a guarantee of fit. Secure the board without covering the light-sensitive face or shorting its underside. Replace the short bench jumpers with a retained four-conductor harness. Keep the ESP32 on the cart and the light board on the paddle. The robot’s supplied servo cables are occupied and are not a spare light-sensor bus. Provide strain relief at the paddle and cart, service loops at joints, and a parked tool rest. Test the entire intended reach while logging sensor errors. If the longer I²C link fails, shorten/rework it before trusting readings. Paddle stays secure and the complete moving harness passes a reach test. Step 11 Finish durable connections and repeatable light measurements On the bench: Perfboard/terminals if needed, insulation, fasteners and tool rest. If using perfboard, solder the headers/terminal pins and required interconnects on the dry bench. Check continuity against the tested circuit. Breadboard contacts are temporary, not a moving-arm connector. Insulate exposed splices with suitable sleeves or enclosed connectors; heat-shrink is only needed where there is an exposed joint. Fasten the electronics clear of water and keep the USB connector accessible. Teach a pose at canopy height with the face upward and the robot out of its light path. Stop moving, collect repeated fresh readings and record pose/time. Park the light tool before picking up a bottle. Lux readings do not directly measure plant-useful PPFD. One reproducible light-reading pose and one reliable tool-rest pose established. The GPIO assignment above is a project proposal for the recorded ESP-WROOM-32 board, not a verified photo of the delivered ELEGOO pinout. Espressif reference . The board’s own pin labels and documentation take precedence. 12–14 · Add trays and supervised watering The water under the cress tray is a small built-in supply. The robot-held bottle replenishes it. An external tank and pump are not part of this setup. Step 12 Assemble and test both growing kits by hand On the bench: Cress trough, holder and four insets; square outer tray and insert; paper and water. Follow the combined growing guide for fit, leak and paper-wick tests. Use the square tray’s printed cover when available, or a loose household cover for the trial. Leave an accessible refill opening and inspection spot. Check that paper wets across the seeded area, not just where it first touches water. The square kit needs an actual capillary connection; simply adding water below an elevated insert does not prove self-watering. Start on a stable household surface. Add the modular printed table only after its actual joints, stiffness and reach are checked. Use repeatable tray locations so a taught pour target does not move. Both trays pass hand-operated leak/wetness checks and sit in repeatable positions. Step 13 Teach an empty bottle pickup and return On the bench: Small bottle, suitable outlet, bottle rest, robot gripper and empty tray. Check grip width and retention with an empty bottle. The selected Nalgene container has a wide mouth: validate a fitted spout or use an existing bottle with a controlled outlet. The rendered spout is not a finished printable design. Place the bottle in a repeatable rest outside the crop. Teach pickup, approach to the refill opening, upright recovery and return while empty. Check wrist-camera view, clearance above the tray rim and cable slack through the whole path. A manual spray bottle is for hand use until trigger actuation is proven. Empty bottle can be picked up, aimed and returned without slipping or colliding. Step 14 Try tiny supervised pours and record results On the bench: Small measured water fill, kitchen measuring container, household catch dish and towel. First pour into a kitchen measure over a catch dish, with a person supervising. Record starting fill, pose and actual water delivered. Repeat across different fill levels; tilt duration alone does not establish a dose. After that works, try a small refill of the empty planter. Check for overflow and verify the paper still receives water. Keep the Mac, hub and sensor electronics clear of the wet area. For the initial crop, a person checks water reserve and paper wetness and authorizes each refill. Cameras record evidence; an obscured view is unknown. Do not replace the removed probe with an unvalidated camera-only autonomous watering rule. Supervised pours and upright recovery work; a human remains responsible for watering decisions. Open the combined growing and kit instructions · Why the moisture probe is optional 15–16 · Add only what the next test needs Step 15 Keep optional sensor parts off the first build On the bench: SHT31, moisture probe, relay modules and moisture-holder prototypes. An optional SHT31 measures air temperature/humidity. If wanted, mount it on the dry body in ventilated air, away from motor/electronics heat; it does not need to ride on the arm. Add it to the verified 3.3V-compatible I²C bus only after checking its labels and address. Defer the SparkFun moisture probe and its power relay for the paper-tray build. They are retained in the reference diagrams for a future comparison experiment, not required connections. If later testing the probe, validate repeated contact on sacrificial paper, switched power, dry/damp/wet discrimination and contamination/cleaning before mounting it near a crop. A water-depth solution is a different experiment. Optional parts explicitly marked installed or deferred; absent probe does not become a fake dry reading. Step 16 Commission battery power and mobility separately On the bench: Owned Anker C300 DC, verified conversion cables/adapters, matched robot inputs. Keep using wall power until the motor power path is checked. The transcript mentions two USB-C PD-to-12V cables, but their actual availability and electrical suitability remain unverified. For every powered device, verify negotiated output voltage, polarity, barrel size, continuous/peak current and simultaneous-port behavior. The hub needs its own matched supply path; it cannot be assumed to run from an arbitrary USB-A port. Secure the battery low on the cart. Test power stability with the full load before untethered driving. Use the two-wheel base profile and a clear area for the first drive test; farm care remains parked. Battery conversion and base motion separately verified, or explicitly deferred. Connection checklist: what plugs into what? Part Destination Mount / joining method Hub upstream cable Mac USB 3-capable port Plug-in; hub secured on dry cart. Motor controller A and B USB Two hub data ports Kit USB cables; label A/B. Separate matched motor supplies. Head + two wrist cameras Three hub data ports Supplied mounts and screws; slack at head/wrist joints. One ESP32 USB Sixth hub data port Data-capable cable; dry enclosure on robot body. Seventh port remains spare. One BH1750 ESP32 3V3, GND, SDA and SCL Printed paddle plus retained four-wire harness; headers may need solder. Optional SHT31 Verified compatible ESP32 I²C bus Body-mounted; optional air context. Moisture probe and relay Not connected in recommended first build Deferred with probe holder and probe-specific harness. Bottle and rest Mechanical grip only; no electrical connection Measured grip and outlet; water added by a person. Planters and table No electrical connection Trays stay on a stable surface; robot reaches them. Perfboard / breadboard / wire / fasteners Support the light circuit and cable retention Bench-test first; solder only loose headers, chosen perfboard interconnects or splices. The full robot uses five hub data ports; the light-sensor controller adds one. No added pump, scale, external reservoir, overhead camera or second computer is needed for this supervised configuration. Remaining physical fit checks: delivered kit revision, paddle/board retention, bottle grip/outlet, enclosure/fasteners and moving cable length. These depend on the actual parts; the existing Blender scenes and tool STLs are prototypes, not evidence that those fits have passed.

title: 9–11 · Add just one light sensor
text: 9–11 · Add just one light sensor Use one BH1750, with its sensing face upward. The ESP32 stays on the dry robot body. The gripper holds the paddle only while taking a reading. Step 09 Wire a short light-sensor circuit on the bench On the bench: One ELEGOO ESP32, one BH1750, USB data cable, breadboard and jumper wires. With USB unplugged, read the labels on both boards. Fit headers only if needed; solder loose headers into their plated holes. Already installed headers require no soldering. For a verified ESP-WROOM-32 board, our proposed assignment is BH1750 VCC to ESP32 3V3, GND to GND, SDA to GPIO21 and SCL to GPIO22. Match by GPIO label, not physical pin number. Confirm the actual breakout accepts 3.3V and its bus pull-ups do not exceed 3.3V. Check for shorts, then power the ESP32 only through its USB data cable from the hub. Configure firmware to the same SDA/SCL pins, detect the sensor and log lux over serial. Cover/uncover the sensor and confirm the reading changes. Light readings reach the Mac and change reliably when shaded. Step 10 Fit the printed paddle and flexible harness On the bench: Light paddle prototype, BH1750, flexible wire, retained connector and dry ESP32 enclosure. Dry-fit the actual board to the paddle; the prototype is not a guarantee of fit. Secure the board without covering the light-sensitive face or shorting its underside. Replace the short bench jumpers with a retained four-conductor harness. Keep the ESP32 on the cart and the light board on the paddle. The robot’s supplied servo cables are occupied and are not a spare light-sensor bus. Provide strain relief at the paddle and cart, service loops at joints, and a parked tool rest. Test the entire intended reach while logging sensor errors. If the longer I²C link fails, shorten/rework it before trusting readings. Paddle stays secure and the complete moving harness passes a reach test. Step 11 Finish durable connections and repeatable light measurements On the bench: Perfboard/terminals if needed, insulation, fasteners and tool rest. If using perfboard, solder the headers/terminal pins and required interconnects on the dry bench. Check continuity against the tested circuit. Breadboard contacts are temporary, not a moving-arm connector. Insulate exposed splices with suitable sleeves or enclosed connectors; heat-shrink is only needed where there is an exposed joint. Fasten the electronics clear of water and keep the USB connector accessible. Teach a pose at canopy height with the face upward and the robot out of its light path. Stop moving, collect repeated fresh readings and record pose/time. Park the light tool before picking up a bottle. Lux readings do not directly measure plant-useful PPFD. One reproducible light-reading pose and one reliable tool-rest pose established. title: 12–14 · Add trays and supervised watering
text: 12–14 · Add trays and supervised watering The water under the cress tray is a small built-in supply. The robot-held bottle replenishes it. An external tank and pump are not part of this setup. Step 12 Assemble and test both growing kits by hand On the bench: Cress trough, holder and four insets; square outer tray and insert; paper and water. Follow the combined growing guide for fit, leak and paper-wick tests. Use the square tray’s printed cover when available, or a loose household cover for the trial. Leave an accessible refill opening and inspection spot. Check that paper wets across the seeded area, not just where it first touches water. Add the modular printed table only after its actual joints, stiffness and reach are checked. Use repeatable tray locations so a taught pour target does not move. Step 13 Teach an empty bottle pickup and return On the bench: Small bottle, suitable outlet, bottle rest, robot gripper and empty tray. Check grip width and retention with an empty bottle. title: 15–16 · Add only what the next test needs
text: 15–16 · Add only what the next test needs Step 15 Keep optional sensor parts off the first build On the bench: SHT31, moisture probe, relay modules and moisture-holder prototypes. The hub needs its own matched supply path; it cannot be assumed to run from an arbitrary USB-A port. Secure the battery low on the cart.
