text: One Mac. Separate motor and sensor connections. The first build keeps the robot parked and uses its existing cameras. Sensors attach through an ESP32; USB does not power the robot’s motors. Open the 16-step robot assembly guide Do these microgreen trays need the soil-moisture probe? No, not for the initial paper-grown trial. We recommend deferring the probe and its relay. Keep one light paddle if you want robotic light measurements. The planters themselves need no electronics. The cress trough stores water below the growing surface. Paper must remain connected to that water. Water in the trough and wetness at the seeds are two separate checks. Question First-build check What the probe would tell us Is there water left below the plants? A person checks the accessible refill area; record a photo when visible. Touching the paper does not measure water depth. Is water reaching the growing surface? Inspect a seed-free edge and check paper wetness by hand with clean hands, without disturbing roots. Repeat at more than one area. Conductivity only at the contact patch, if contact is repeatable. Should the robot refill? A person reviews both checks and authorizes a small tested pour. A reading alone cannot establish the needed dose or rule out wick failure. The SparkFun guide describes a resistive conductivity measurement and recommends powering only for readings to reduce corrosion. On our thin paper, contact pressure, contact area and water chemistry can change the result. That makes it an optional experiment, not a validated requirement. It might become useful with thicker growing media or a demonstrably repeatable paper contact method. For the square kit: do not assume the perforated insert wicks by itself. Establish the paper/mat’s capillary connection by hand before depending on water beneath it. A full lower tray can coexist with a dry growing surface. For future unattended care: removing the probe does not make cameras a proven replacement. Water-level visibility, a validated level sensor/indicator, or another independent measurement could be evaluated later. A hidden waterline or uncertain wetness pauses automatic watering. Neither a level reading alone nor a timer proves that the wick is working. Shopping implication: propose deferring the $14.45 probe and $8.99 relay pack ($23.44 at the last recorded prices). One sentence: A Python program on the Mac that turns the robot kit into a plant caretaker nobody drives: the model teaches it, rules and Jev decide, a person is asked only when needed. Exists · LeRobot / XLeRobot We build Deferred Human Scope One parked robot, two arms, three cameras, one light sensor, cress trays in fixed printed nests, one bottle. Nobody drives the robot. Status Layers 1–7 exist as code in software/ (Sep 27): 37 tests pass; Claude CLI, Jev and Astra verified live; STOP, cup-test, bus probe, Telegram and run recording added. Untested on the physical robot until Sep 30. Navigate Arrow keys or the buttons. O opens the outline; P presents full screen. Sources: XLeRobot repository and docs, LeRobot 0.6.1, the September 20 redline, the software/ package and its tests. Why write anything at all · 02 / 20 The kit is a body with reflexes. The farm needs a routine, a memory and a conscience. XLeRobot gives us motors, cameras, kinematics and a way to train policies. It does not know what a tray is. What the kit does out of the box XLeRobot + LeRobot today • A person drives the arms, head and wheels with a keyboard, Xbox pad, Joy-Cons or VR. • Three cameras stream frames; joint positions read back 30× per second. • Demonstrations can be recorded to a dataset and a policy (ACT / SmolVLA / π0.5) trained on them. • An LLM-agent example turns camera + tools into “approach a human”. It has no idea what a tray, a plant, water, a schedule, a fault or “yesterday” is. The plant-watering clip in the showcase is teleoperated, sped up 8×. What a farm caretaker needs The farm program • Knows which tray it is looking at and whether the view is fresh. • Runs a fixed routine: inspect → measure → ask → pour → verify → park. • Asks a person before water moves; pours a bounded amount; returns upright. • Writes down intent, attempt and outcome before, during and after every action. • Pauses on doubt and never repeats a pour whose result is unknown. • Lets a person see why it paused and fix it from a screen. • Gets better from its own recorded episodes, in the open. the gap = this deck Exists Teleoperation, calibration, dataset recording, policy training. All Python on a laptop. Missing A schedule, tray identity, human authorization, bounded pouring, a record of what happened, pause-on-doubt, and a screen for a person. Therefore We write a farm layer on top of LeRobot and call the robot object directly. We do not fork the robot code. The showcase watering clip (0:56–0:59) is labelled “Teleoped with Switch Joycons”. No plant-care policy or checkpoint was found in the upstream repo or on the Hugging Face Hub. The physical system · 03 / 20 Everything is a USB device on one Mac Two motor boards, three cameras and one ESP32 plug into a powered hub. Motor power is separate wall supplies. MacBook Neo Runs everything. No Raspberry Pi. Python · LeRobot · our farm code RSHTECH 7-port hub Own 5 V adapter. Carries USB data only. Never powers motors. One interface for every device read() → {value, t, seq, status} status ∈ { OK, STALE, INVALID, NOT_APPLICABLE } — nothing upstream ever sees a bare number Robot adapter Wraps XLerobot2Wheels. joints(), frames(), move_to(targets, max_step), stop(), torque_off(). Every frame carries capture time. Old frame → STALE. No device → INVALID. Config decides what exists enabled: robot, cameras, esp32_light disabled: sht31, moisture, wheels, pump A disabled device reads NOT_APPLICABLE forever. Why this layer first The simulator implements the same four interfaces with fakes, so the whole program above runs on the Mac before the robot exists. Swapping fake → real is one line in the config. Robot Wraps XLerobot2Wheels. Adds per-tick load and temperature checks, a clamped move_to, and stop / torque_off. Cameras Bound by device identity, not by index — indices reshuffle on reconnect. Every frame carries its capture time. ESP32 Firmware prints one JSON line per reading with a sequence number. A gap or silence becomes STALE on the Mac side; an I²C error becomes INVALID. Human Buttons in the viewer are an input device too: each press is a named, timestamped record. NOT_APPLICABLE is the state of a device the config disabled. The orchestrator can plan around it; it can never treat it as a reading. “No probe” is not “dry”. Layer 2 · 08 / 20 Skills: eight motions with contracts, taught by the model Each skill states what must be true before it runs and what is true after. The orchestrator only ever calls skills, never joints. Nobody drives the arm to teach them. Skill Needs before True after Arm go_rest() any arms at rest pose, grippers as-is both look_at(tray) tray known head + wrist cameras framed on tray head pick_tool(paddle | bottle) gripper empty, tool in rest tool gripped; grip verified by gripper position one arm measure_pose(tray) paddle gripped paddle level at canopy height, arm out of light left pour(tray, tilt°, s) bottle gripped, fill known, human OK tilt held for s seconds, then upright right return_upright() bottle gripped bottle vertical; commanded before any release right place_tool() tool gripped, rest free tool in rest, gripper open, arm clear one arm stop() any motion halted; torque held or off per rule both v1 · keyframes taught by the vision model (implemented) The LLM-servo loop drives the arm in clamped steps from the wrist and head views until the goal is visibly met, then saves the joints as a named keyframe. No person touches a controller. Every skill replays keyframes under the safety rules and checks its own postcondition. v2 · learned policies (later, from the robot’s own runs) Record the robot’s successful keyframe runs with lerobot-record, train ACT, run it behind the same skill interface. Only replaces a v1 skill after it wins on held-out episodes. Still no human demonstrations. LLM-servo farm teach-all: for each needed pose the vision model sees the wrist and head views and returns one clamped step (≤15 mm, ≤6°) until it says done; the reached joints become a keyframe. Verified live on the simulator: 4 steps → done → keyframe saved. Contracts pick_tool verifies the grip from the gripper position; pour() refuses without a gripped bottle and an authorization record; return_upright() is commanded before any release. v2 A skill may later be replaced by an ACT policy trained on the robot’s own recorded runs, behind the same interface, after it wins on held-out episodes. Pour parameters are tilt angle and seconds, calibrated into a kitchen measuring cup (farm calibrate-pour). A tilt duration is never recorded as millilitres. Layer 3 · 09 / 20 Perception: six outputs, each with an unknown From three frames, joint positions and the lux stream, perception answers a fixed set of questions with typed values. Inputs 3 frames + capture time current joint positions ESP32 lux stream tray_id which tray, from its fixed nest position (+ optional AprilTag) ↳ UNKNOWN if the nest is empty or the view is off fresh frame age < 1 s and camera matches its name ↳ STALE otherwise; nothing downstream runs on stale opening_visible refill opening clear and reachable in the wrist view ↳ UNKNOWN if occluded or dark spill CLEAR / SPILL / UNKNOWN around the tray after a pour ↳ an unseen area can never be CLEAR growth green-pixel fraction from the same head pose each day ↳ a trend for people, not a decision input light median lux, spread, saturation over ~10 fresh conversions ↳ INVALID if arm shadow or sensor error The one rule Every output has an UNKNOWN value and the cycle treats UNKNOWN as “stop and ask”, never as “fine”. v1 → v2 v1: OpenCV colour / tag / difference checks. v2: a vision model on the same frames. Same typed outputs. Identity Trays live in fixed nests, so tray_id comes from position; AprilTags are an optional upgrade for trays that move. Freshness A frame older than one second, or from a camera that is not the one its name claims, blocks the cycle. Spill Three values. An area the camera cannot see is UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN after a pour pauses the cycle for a human look. Growth and light Green fraction and lux statistics are for people and for cohort comparison. They never decide a pour. v1 is OpenCV: nest occupancy, colour and frame differencing. v2 may be a vision model, but it must return the same typed outputs. Camera spill detection is experimental and gets its own fault tests. Layer 4 · 10 / 20 The care cycle: a state machine that would rather stop than guess Eleven states, one decision gate, two ways to pause. Every arrow requires named evidence and has a deadline. IDLE IDENTIFY INSPECT MEASURE LIGHT DECIDE PICK BOTTLE APPROACH POUR RETURN UPRIGHT VERIFY PARK evidence + deadline on every arrow rules → Jev → person · no “yes” → PARK, no water PAUSED (reason, evidence) Any check fails, any deadline passes, any adapter goes INVALID or STALE. Motors stop; bottle is returned upright first if it is held. UNKNOWN DELIVERY Crash or lost acknowledgement between POUR and VERIFY. Stays UNKNOWN until a person reconciles. Automatic retry is not an option. Human review Re-inspect, confirm physically, authorize, resolve, or take over. Only a person leaves PAUSED. Deadlines (profile): identify 10 s · inspect 20 s · measure 15 s · decide/ask 10 min · pick 30 s · pour ≤ 4 s tilt · verify 20 s · park 30 s. Implemented in farm/cycle/. Happy path identify → inspect → measure light → decide → pick bottle → approach → pour → return upright → verify → park. The gate DECIDE runs the rules, then Jev, then — only if authority requires it — asks a person in the viewer. No answer within the deadline means park, not pour. Pause Any failed check or timed-out step enters PAUSED with its reason and evidence. Only a person leaves it. Unknown A crash between the tilt and the verify leaves the pour UNKNOWN. The cycle will not retry; a person reconciles. Deadlines are starting values in the config. Pick / dock / weigh states from the redline belong to a future pod-moving profile and are not in this machine. Layer 5 · 11 / 20 Evidence store: intent, attempt, outcome — in that order SQLite for metadata, files for images, append-only everywhere. “We sent the command” and “water reached the tray” are separate rows. cycles cycle_id, tray_id, profile, code_version, config_hash, calibration_id, simulated, started, ended, result observations obs_id, cycle_id, source, t, status, value_json, image_hash, extractor_version decisions decision_id, cycle_id, kind (rule | human | jev_shadow), inputs_ref, choice, probabilities, schema_version actions action_id, cycle_id, skill, params, INTENT_t, ATTEMPT_t, RESULT ∈ {VERIFIED, ABORTED, UNKNOWN}, VERIFY_t, evidence_ref interventions who, t, what was physically checked, what was done, minutes spent One pour, written three times INTENT written before any motor command ATTEMPT written before the tilt can move water VERIFY written after the wrist camera confirms crash here → RESULT = UNKNOWN Rules Append-only. Images stored by content hash, never overwritten. Duplicate action_id returns the existing record — the database cannot make a pour happen exactly once, only refuse to pretend. Nightly backup with a restore test. What the store never contains A number without a status and a time. An estimated volume labelled as measured. “Delivered” inferred from “the servo finished moving”. Secrets, network credentials or addresses. Five tables cycles, observations, decisions, actions, interventions. Every row carries code version, config hash and calibration id. Three writes per pour INTENT before any motor command, ATTEMPT before the tilt can move water, VERIFY after the camera confirms. A crash in between reads as UNKNOWN forever. Never A value without a status and time; an estimate labelled as measured; “delivered” inferred from “servo finished”; any secret. Idempotent action ids stop a restart from double-recording; they cannot stop physics from double-pouring. That is why UNKNOWN blocks retries. Nightly backup includes a restore test. Layer 6a · 12 / 20 The exception viewer: the reason, the evidence and the eligible next steps A local web page on the Mac. When the robot pauses it shows the latest frame, its age, the reason and only the actions that are safe. localhost:8765 · farm viewer · tray B · cycle 0042 latest wrist frame age 0.6 s · right_wrist PAUSED reason: spill = UNKNOWN after pour (area under the rim not visible from right_wrist) last verified: RETURN_UPRIGHT ✓ 12:04:31 · fill ~40 mL (human, 11:58) evidence: obs 9124 · action 771 · decision rule:spill_gate Eligible next steps Re-inspect from head camera I looked: no spill, paper wet I looked: spill — cleaned, resolved Caretaker takes over this tray Retry pour — not offered while delivery is UNKNOWN Every press → intervention record: who, when, what was checked. Shadow (later): Jev suggested inspect_water 0.71 — logged, not acted on. Local network only. Not a safety device — stop rules live in the controller. Shows Current state, last verified action, why it paused, which observation and rule produced the pause. Offers Re-inspect, confirm a physical check, authorize one pour, mark resolved, hand the tray to a caretaker. Each press becomes an intervention record. Never offers Retry pour while delivery is UNKNOWN. The button does not exist in that state. Reachable from a phone on the same Wi-Fi; not exposed to the internet. Not a safety device — the stop rules run in the controller whether or not anyone is looking. Layer 6b · 13 / 20 Jev and Astra: authority earned from the first cycles Rules own protection and can only say no. Jev answers typed questions and climbs a ladder; Astra reviews the day and proposes. Neither can move a servo. Evidence packet tray_id, age, recent pours, sensor statuses, image features, device faults, last action, allowed next steps. Small, typed, timestamped. Local rules (must pass) Numeric bounds, freshness, device health, human authorization present. Own machine protection. Run without any network. Gate → one preapproved skill Only a skill from the allowed list can execute, and only if rules passed. A model label is never permission to move or pour. Jev · typesafe/jev-router (live) next_review → routine | inspect_water | inspect_image | review_machine | review_hygiene | unknown pour_decision → pour | skip | reinspect | unknown Choice + probabilities; unknown on any failure. suggestion only, logged Astra · openai/gpt-6-astra (live) Reads the last 24 h of evidence: results, pauses, unknowns, minutes, disagreements, cost. Proposes one change with evidence, expected benefit and rollback. apply-safe may change only whitelisted numbers inside bounds. Never writes servo commands. Never on the protection path. Human caretaker Physical checks, authorizations, ambiguous crop calls, final incident labels. The only party that leaves PAUSED. The authority ladder (implemented): shadow → route → approve Starts in shadow: Jev is asked and recorded, a person authorizes. After jev_shadow_cycles with ≥80% route agreement it promotes to route (Jev’s reinspect/pause routes are honoured). After another run with every pour decision agreeing with the person it promotes to approve: Jev may authorize a routine pour when rules pass and p ≥ 0.85; people are notified, not asked. A spill at reconciliation demotes it. Any person can set the level from the viewer. Jev Two questions per packet with images — next review and pour decision — each with probabilities and an explicit unknown. Live via OpenRouter typesafe/jev-router (~$0.002 per call). Ladder shadow → route → approve, promoted automatically on agreement with the rules and the person; demoted on a false approval. At approve, Jev authorizes routine pours (p ≥ 0.85) and people are notified. Astra farm review reads 24 h of evidence and proposes one change with rollback; apply-safe may change only whitelisted numbers inside bounds (deadlines, light sampling, a stricter Jev threshold). Tested: shadow records but does not honour; approve authorizes without asking; low probability still asks; promotion and demotion. Cloud calls stay off the protection path; the daily budget blocks pours when exhausted. Layer 7 · 14 / 20 The learning loop: the model teaches, the robot’s own runs train No human demonstrations. The LLM-servo teaches keyframes; successful keyframe runs are the dataset; crop learning is A/B cohorts with one difference at a time. LLM-servo vision model drives the arm to each goal; keyframe saved lerobot-record record the robot’s own successful runs (no human demos) LeRobotDataset parquet + mp4, our tray, our bottle, our poses Train ACT on the Mac or a rented GPU; version the checkpoint Offline replay candidate vs v1 keyframe skill on held-out episodes Shadow policy proposes, keyframes execute; log disagreement Limited pilot empty bottle, then cup, then tray; rollback ready Robot learning: the model teaches v1; the robot’s own runs train v2 Crop learning: recipes change between frozen cohorts, never inside one Cohort A · Sep 30 Cress on paper, recipe A. Every pour, light reading and human minute recorded. Cohort B · Oct 3 Same seed lot, one deliberate difference (e.g. light position). Same records. Proposal C Astra summarises A vs B and proposes one change with a rollback condition. A person accepts or not. What is honest to say today No pretrained watering policy exists anywhere we looked; the two “water” datasets on the Hub are bottle transport. The upstream demo is teleoperated. Training happens on our own episodes or not at all, and logging alone improves nothing. Robot LLM-servo → keyframes → the robot’s own runs recorded (farm run --record, LeRobotDataset v3) → ACT on the Mac or SmolVLA on a rented GPU → offline eval → farm policy-test on the sim, then the robot, under the same clamps → shadow → limited pilot. Prior data Same-arm SO-101 pouring datasets exist (best: UNITAmanipulation/so101_pour_water, 100 episodes, wrist + top cameras); an ACT pipeline check on SurajCreation/so101_pour_v1 ran on this Mac. They teach the pour motion prior; the last 10–20 cm to our tray must come from our own episodes. Crop Cohort A on Sep 30, B on Oct 3 from the same seed lot. Astra proposes C from their records; a person decides. Discipline Simulated and real episodes are never mixed. Nothing is tuned on the evaluation set. A recipe never changes mid-cohort except as a recorded deviation. No pretrained watering policy exists for XLeRobot (its “water” datasets fetch a bottle); the full survey of 57 datasets and 16 checkpoints is in software/docs/research-training.md. Training on our own runs is optional inside the trip. End to end · 15 / 20 One cycle, thirteen messages, seven lanes Follow a single authorized pour from the first camera frame to the shadow classification. Hardware Adapters Perception Orchestrator Evidence Human Jev (shadow) 1. read joints, 3 frames, lux 2. observations with status 3. tray B · fresh · opening visible · light 410 lx 4. decision: rules pass → ASK_HUMAN 5. viewer: “tray B looks dry at edge — authorize 1 pour?” 6. authorize (name, time) → intervention record 7. action INTENT pour(B, 35°, 2 s) 8. skill pick_bottle → approach → pour 9. send_action(joint targets, clamped) 10. ATTEMPT written before tilt 11. spill CLEAR · opening wet → VERIFIED 12. RESULT VERIFIED · PARK 13. packet → “routine” 0.88 (logged only) 1–4 Adapters read; perception judges tray B fresh and reachable; rules pass; the orchestrator decides to ask. 5–6 At shadow/route level the viewer shows the frame and a person authorizes; at approve level Jev authorizes (p ≥ 0.85) and the person is only notified. 7–10 INTENT, then skills, then clamped joint targets, then ATTEMPT — written before the tilt. 11–13 Perception verifies wetness and no spill; result VERIFIED; the packet goes to Jev in shadow. Replace step 11 with “spill UNKNOWN” and the cycle enters PAUSED; replace a crash between 10 and 11 and the action stays UNKNOWN. Both paths are on the state-machine slide. Building it before the robot exists · 16 / 20 The simulator is the same program with fakes plugged in Because everything above layer 1 talks to adapters, fakes make the whole farm program runnable on the Mac this week. Farm program (unchanged) orchestrator perception evidence store viewer skills Adapter interface read() → status move_to() frames() lux() confirm() Real devices XLerobot2Wheels OpenCV cameras ESP32 serial browser buttons Fakes FakeRobot: kinematic model, instant or slow FakeCamera: replays saved frames FakeESP32: scripted lux FakeHuman: scripted answers Fault injection stale frame camera unplugged serial gap servo overtemp crash after ATTEMPT human never answers wrong tray in nest lost acknowledgement Every simulated record carries simulated = true, so fake episodes can never be counted as farm evidence. This is what gets built first, on the Mac, before the robot exists — and it stays as the regression suite forever. Fakes FakeRobot with a kinematic model, FakeCamera replaying saved frames, FakeESP32 with scripted lux, FakeHuman with scripted answers. Faults Stale frames, unplugged camera, serial gaps, overtemp, crash after ATTEMPT, silent human, wrong tray. Each has a test. Forever The fakes become the regression suite. Every later change to the orchestrator runs against them first. All simulated records carry simulated = true. They are never counted as farm evidence or used to tune thresholds for the real system. Config, safety, deferrals · 17 / 20 One profile names what exists; code enforces what may move The config profile lists ports, camera identities, tray nests and enabled sensors. Safety limits are code and outrank every model. profile: paper-tray-v0 robot: port1: /dev/tty.usbmodem58A6… port2: /dev/tty.usbmodem58B1… max_relative_target: 8 wheels: disabled cameras: head: {id: "USB Camera 0C45:6366-1"} right_wrist: {id: "…-2"} sensors: {esp32_light: on, sht31: off, moisture: off} trays: B: {nest: right_front, pour_pose: kf_pour_B_v3} limits: {tilt_max: 40, pour_s_max: 4, temp_max: 55} Local safety rules (code, not config) Joint range from calibration; refuse targets outside it. Max step per tick — the arm cannot jump. Servo temperature / load ceiling → stop. Watchdog: no fresh observation for 0.5 s → stop. Disconnect → torque off (upstream default), after return_upright if a bottle is held. No model output can relax any of these. Deferred — exists in the design, off in V0 Base driving and battery power. Pump, relay, moisture probe, scale, leak pads. Fixed overhead camera. Printer pickup, table construction. Any pour without a human “yes”. Each returns when its own test passes; nothing is promised by date. Profile paper-tray-v0: two serial ports, three camera identities, esp32_light on, everything else off, tray B with its nest and pour keyframe. Safety Calibrated joint ranges, max step per tick, servo temperature ceiling, 0.5 s watchdog, torque-off on disconnect after upright. Deferred Driving, battery, pump, probe, scale, overhead camera, printer pickup, unsupervised pouring. Each returns when its own test passes. A wrong profile is the most likely way to hurt the robot: the assembly guide’s port-discovery and calibration steps come before the first move. Build order · 18 / 20 Five phases, five gates, Sep 26 → Oct 10 — Phase 0 done Phase 0 (Mac-only) finished Sep 27. Each later phase opens only when the previous gate passes; a failed gate holds the previous level. Phase 0 ✓ Sep 26–27 · Mac only · DONE no robot yet • adapters real + fakes • evidence store + schema • care cycle on simulator • viewer • ESP32 firmware + parser • Jev/Astra/Claude live Gate passed: full fake cycle, crash-after-ATTEMPT → UNKNOWN, 23 tests Phase 1 Sep 30–Oct 2 · connect robot in Japan • assemble, farm devices, calibrate • farm check: views verified • farm teach-all (LLM-servo) • empty-bottle farm once Gate: empty bottle picked, aimed, returned 10/10; stop works Phase 2 Oct 3–5 · one real cycle water moves • cup pours → calibrate-pour • full cycle on the tray, person authorizes • Jev in shadow, promoting on evidence Gate: 5 cycles, every record complete, zero unknown left open Phase 3 Oct 6–8 · observe + record longer windows • farm run --every 3600 • Jev at route → approve • Astra daily review + proposals • record own runs Gate: alerts fire on injected faults during a real window Phase 4 Oct 9–10 · hand over someone else runs it • offline eval vs rules • export dataset + incident bundle • caretaker runbook, restore test Gate: another person resolves a staged exception A failed gate holds the previous level. Dates are targets; the gates are the plan. Status on Sep 27 Phase 0 is done: software/ holds layers 1–7, 37 tests pass, and the Claude CLI, Jev router and Astra were exercised live; the step-by-step guide covers every remaining physical step. Nothing has touched the physical robot yet; every claim about reach, grip and pours waits for Sep 30. Phase 0 · done Sep 27 Adapters, fakes, evidence store, care cycle on the simulator, viewer, ESP32 firmware, live model checks. Gate passed: a fake cycle survives a crash after ATTEMPT; 23 tests. Phase 1 · Sep 30–Oct 2 Assemble, farm devices → calibrate → check (camera identities confirmed by the model) → teach-all (LLM-servo) → empty-bottle farm once. Gate: 10/10 pick-aim-return and a working stop. Phase 2 · Oct 3–5 Measured pours into a cup, then the full cycle on a real tray with the human gate. Gate: five complete supervised cycles, nothing UNKNOWN left open. Phases 3–4 · Oct 6–10 Observation windows 2 → 8 → 24 h, demo recording, first training attempt, offline eval, caretaker handover. The printed trays and nests do not exist yet (M5C prints pending), so Phase 2 assumes they are printed by Oct 3 or a household tray sits in a taped-down position. Fixed trays · 19 / 20 Trays live in printed nests; the printer is an AnkerMake M5C A locating plate per cress planter gives the software a tray identity without vision, a repeatable pour pose, and a recess for an AprilTag if trays ever move. Paddle and bottle rest are printed too. table top (printed modular table or any stable surface) tag A refill notch nest_cress.stl · tray A 200 × 165 · pocket 181.5 × 86.5 3 stepped ledges · 6 mm lip tag B refill notch nest_cress.stl · tray B 200 × 165 · pocket 181.5 × 86.5 3 stepped ledges · 6 mm lip bottle_rest.stl · Ø70, 56 mm bore paddle_bh1750.stl · 150 × 24 × 8 · sensor pocket robot cart parks here → AnkerMake M5C 220 × 220 × 250 mm · 0.4 mm · PLA Cress planter: fits (180 × 85). Square kit outer tray 220 × 220: does not fit — 95% scale or drop. Why nests tray_id comes from the nest, not from vision; the tag recess is the optional upgrade for trays that move. One taught pour pose per nest stays valid across cycles. Files (generated, verified) 5 STLs: nest 200×165×10, tag id1/id2 40×40×1.6 (real 36h11 patterns), paddle 150×24×8, rest Ø70×12. Every STL re-parsed: size = 84 + 50·triangles. Nest plate 200 × 165 × 10 mm: 181.5 × 86.5 pocket with three stepped ledges as lead-in, 6 mm lip, a 48 mm front apron carrying the 40.5 × 40.5 tag recess and two M4 holes, two rear tabs, a 30 mm spout notch. Fits the bed. Tags, paddle, rest AprilTag 36h11 id 1 and id 2 as 40 × 40 × 1.6 tiles with raised cells (patterns verified against the library code words). Paddle 150 × 24 × 8 with grip grooves, BH1750 pocket, cable channel. Bottle rest Ø70 × 12, 56 mm bore, 40° lead-in. Fit Cress planter and all new parts fit the 220 × 220 bed. The square kit’s 220 × 220 outer tray does not; print it at 95% or leave it out. Generated by software/parts/make_parts.py (pure-numpy STL writer, self-checked). Its README lists ten assumptions to verify: bottle diameter (54 mm), BH1750 hole spacing (14.5 mm), trough size (180 × 85), tile clearance, and that raised tag cells are made black (filament change at Z = 1.0 mm or marker). Decisions taken · Sep 27 · 20 / 20 Six decisions, settled These are now in the profile and the code. Change any line and the affected slides and modules update. 1 · No human operation Nobody drives the robot. People answer questions in the viewer; that is all. ↳ Keyframes are taught by the vision model (LLM-servo). Calibration remains a one-time setup step. 2 · Fixed trays + printed nests Printed locating plates hold the cress planters in known positions with an AprilTag recess; printed paddle and bottle rest. ↳ Sized for the AnkerMake M5C. The square kit’s 220 mm tray does not fit that bed. 3 · Arms Right arm = bottle, left arm = light paddle. ↳ Keeps the pour arm’s wrist camera on the opening. 4 · Jev / Astra authority now Ladder shadow → route → approve promotes itself on evidence from the first cycles; Astra proposes daily, apply-safe for bounded numbers. ↳ A person can demote at any time; a spill demotes automatically. 5 · Viewer + light sensor Local web page on the Mac; ESP32 + BH1750 stay in V0. ↳ Firmware and serial adapter are written. 6 · Learning The model teaches; the robot’s own runs are the training data. No ACT training during the trip unless cycles are boring. ↳ Backends: Claude CLI on the subscription for vision; OpenRouter for Jev and Astra. Operation No human operation. The vision model teaches every keyframe; people only answer questions in the viewer (or over chat via the webhook). Authority Jev and Astra earn authority from the first cycles through the ladder; safety rules still outrank them and a person can demote at any time. Not up for debate in V0 Water needs rules + (a person or Jev at approve); UNKNOWN blocks retry; the base stays parked; models never write joint commands. The deck is generated from one Python file (handbook/roadmap.py); the program from software/farm. ← → move · O outline · P present · Esc exit · Print shows every slide. text: What the community changes A review of the 43 projects on the XLeRobot community page against our plan: what is useful, where it lands in the farm program, and what gets built on this Mac as the training and policy server. ← 01 / 11 → Outline Present 01 43 community projects, 7 that matter, 8 changes to our software Community page review · Oct 2 02 Each useful project touches one layer; four layers do not change Where it lands 03 Two computers: one holds the robot, one holds the model This Mac as the GPU server 04 Bring-up: the agent runs the checks, you do the parts that need hands Built today 05 Calibration: keep the hand sweep, add a report, hold the automatic option Calibration 06 Teaching: the model first, your hands only as a chosen fallback Teaching 07 A trained policy is served from this Mac and clamped on the robot Learning 08 A soak test before the robot is left alone Endurance 09 An MCP door that stops at the skill layer Agent access 10 Five rules untouched, two with a new option What does not change 11 Done today, built next, and three decisions for you Plan Community page review · Oct 2 · 01 / 11 43 community projects, 7 that matter, 8 changes to our software Most of the page is about people driving the robot. What is left sharpens bring-up, calibration, teaching and training, without touching the safety model. Two of the eight changes are already built. 43 entries on the XLeRobot community page 7 · useful xlerobot-onboard (installer + Claude skill) RoboCrew (LLM agent loop) xlerobot-mcp (MCP tool server) Dexbotic (training for our exact robot) Kinesthetic recorder (teach by hand) XLeRobot-Pro measurement tools Home Service Demo (grasp checkpoint) 9 · related, nothing to take AnchorVLA4D: pours on an XLeRobot, but no data, code or weights linked Matcha Bot: liquid handling, no dataset Perception Engine: head tracking of people Laundry Bot, OneRobotAI, Grievous, XS-VLA MakerMods parts, Cutting the Cord 27 · not relevant 12 teleoperation (VR, Joy-Con, leader arms, ROS 2) 4 simulation (Isaac, Gazebo, LeHome) 3 different hardware (other arms, lift) 5 voice agents and other stacks 3 unrelated papers Plus one find that is not on the page LeRobot pull request #3282: automatic calibration for SO-101 arms. Open, not merged. Found through xlerobot-onboard. Built and pushed To build Needs a person or a decision Unchanged / not used Checked Every entry’s summary, and the README of the eleven closest. Nothing was installed or run on the robot. Biggest gap found Nobody has published watering or pouring data for this robot. The one paper that pours on an XLeRobot released nothing. Full list software/docs/community-projects.md in the repo. An earlier message said 28 entries were not relevant; the correct count is 27 (one project was counted twice). Where it lands · 02 / 11 Each useful project touches one layer; four layers do not change Perception, the care cycle, the viewer and the authority ladder are untouched. The changes sit at the bottom (devices, calibration) and the top (training). Our stack What the community page adds to each layer 7 · Learning loop policy server on this Mac Dexbotic path · rented NVIDIA 6 · Review · viewer, Jev, Astra unchanged 5 · Evidence store soak-test log taught_by field 4 · Care-cycle orchestrator unchanged 3 · Perception unchanged 2 · Skills remote policy skill by-hand teach · fallback 1 · Device adapters robot-test calibration report auto-calibration · gated 0 · Hardware + upstream bring-up skill New side door farm mcp: any MCP client (Claude Code on the robot laptop) can read state, look through a camera, and run named skills. No raw joint writes. Untouched Safety rules, authority ladder, UNKNOWN handling, parked base. Nothing from the community page relaxes them. Built and pushed To build Needs a person or a decision Unchanged / not used Bottom Bring-up skill and robot-test are built. The calibration report is next; automatic calibration is gated. Middle A remote policy skill, and teaching by hand as a fallback. Top This Mac becomes the training and policy server. Side An MCP door so an agent on the robot laptop can look and run named skills. Tags show intent. Only the two green ones exist today. This Mac as the GPU server · 03 / 11 Two computers: one holds the robot, one holds the model The robot laptop keeps every safety decision. This Mac trains on the robot’s recorded runs and answers “what next?” over the network. Robot laptop · plugged into the robot farm run --record Skills, clamps, STOP, evidence Cameras, motor boards, light sensor over USB Sends: joint state + 3 camera frames Receives: the next 50 actions Every action still passes the clamps here This Mac · M4 Max, 128 GB · the GPU server Trains ACT (and SmolVLA) with LeRobot on Apple GPU farm policy-server: loads a checkpoint, answers /act Offline evaluation against held-out episodes Never touches a motor Holds no robot calibration Can be switched off: the robot falls back to keyframes recorded episodes observation action chunk same Wi-Fi If the link drops The skill stops, holds position and reports. It does not replay stale actions and never assumes the pour happened. Dexbotic (the pipeline for our exact robot) Needs Ubuntu and NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 4090 / A100 class). Not runnable on this Mac. Our recorder already writes the format it converts from, so it stays a rented-GPU option. Built and pushed To build Needs a person or a decision Unchanged / not used Why split Training and a large policy would compete with the control loop on the robot laptop. An M4 Max with 128 GB handles ACT comfortably; the earlier pipeline test trained 5,000 steps here in about an hour. title: Growing trial & kits
text: Two printed kits. One growing trial, not yet started. Understand the water paths, set up the kits, and run the first cress trial when the parts exist. Keep the crop in the kit you sowed it in; transplanting is not required. Wicking planter Square kit Robot access Status Setup Daily care Troubleshooting Notebook Rectangular self-watering cress planter 6 printed pieces What each piece does Trough: stores the small supply of water. Holder: supports the growing paper above it. Four insets: hold paper down into water and make wick paths. They are not four separate crop pots. Trough envelope from the downloaded STL: approximately 180 × 85 × 25 mm. Paper and water are not printed parts. Capillary action does the work A continuous sheet of paper carries water from the trough to the seed platform. Four insets keep the paper in contact with water. Refill before the wick loses contact. Passive watering reduces intervention; it does not guarantee the planter can be left alone for six days. Actual creator meshes cut open for explanation. Household paper connects the seed platform to the stored water; the four insets are wick holders. The cutaway is not a print file. Open the image for a larger view. Original by Macce · CC BY-SA 4.0 . The creator uses household paper and printed PETG; our PLA version needs its own leak and durability checks. Follow the start guide . Square germination tray kit Original downloaded meshes, separated in Blender to explain their roles. Cover orientation depends on its intended use; use it over the growing insert for early germination. Part Function Downloaded envelope A · Cover / part 3 Retains humidity and blocks light initially; remove for the green growth stage. Weighted blackout is crop-specific and not needed for our first cress trial. 205 × 205 × 35 mm B · Insert / part 2 Holds medium/seeds; perforations provide drainage/root access. 195 × 195 × 35 mm C · Outer tray / part 1 Supports the insert and catches or holds water. 220 × 220 × 50 mm These measured STL bounds differ from the listing’s nominal dimensions. Use the downloaded dimensions for print planning. Seed on a suitable moist medium in B; C is not a signal to flood the seeds. If there is an air gap to bottom water, top-wet initially and verify the medium’s water path. Original by HomestteadAce · CC BY-SA 4.0 . Both kits can stay on an ordinary stable household surface for the New York trial. How the robot joins this later Recognize the tray and the saved watering target while its base is parked. Inspect the uncovered crop; a person checks water reserve and wetness at an unseeded paper edge. The contact probe is optional. Use one removable light paddle at plant height as a separate operation. Take a small bottle, pour a tested amount at an accessible target and return upright. Observe wetness/spills and save evidence. Uncertain delivery pauses the cycle. Manual lid removal, bottle refill and tool loading are acceptable V0 steps. The cress refill hole is narrow; the square tray’s access around its fitted insert also needs physical testing. Neither a render nor the upstream demo proves these targets are reachable with our bottle. Why a water pocket if the robot waters? The pocket is inside the planter; the robot can refill it. We removed the separate powered irrigation system, not the plant’s ability to hold water. Where the trial stands September 26: the planned New York pre-trial did not happen. The K1 Max jammed with PLA in the nozzle after the first job was aborted, so no planter part is available and no leak, wick or germination test has been run. The cress seed packet was added to the cart but its purchase is unconfirmed. Everything below is a plan for the first trial, not a record of one. Garden cress ( Lepidium sativum ) suits a small paper-based trial. A seed supplier gives roughly 2–4 days to germinate and 7–10 days to harvest ; real timing varies. Seedmart’s cress guide . This is a planning estimate, not a guarantee for any particular packet. If the kits are not printed by sowing day: use a shallow household dish with household paper. The robot software does not depend on the printed geometry for its first supervised pours; it depends on a tray in a repeatable position with a visible refill opening. Seeds must be bought locally in Japan; carrying seed or growing material through customs is not planned. Your first setup, step by step No moisture electronics are required: check water reserve and paper wetness by hand for this trial. Why we recommend deferring the soil probe . Use what you already have The printed cress planter or square kit once they exist; otherwise a shallow household dish. Fresh garden-cress seed. Use untreated seed intended for growing; check the delivered packet. Plain, unscented household kitchen paper and clean water. A clean kitchen tray/dish underneath, a small cup or spoon, and a phone camera. A household loose cover if the cress planter needs humidity retention; square kit includes its cover. No growing soil, fertilizer, purchased mats, sensors or robot needed for this short paper trial. What “self-watering” means The rectangular planter stores a little water below the seeds. Paper carries it upward by capillary action. You still check it and refill by hand. The square kit has a cover and removable insert, but it does not automatically wick unless its growing medium makes the needed connection to water. See the planter renders Inspect, rinse and leak-test Remove loose plastic, rinse with cool water and check the fit without forcing clips. Put the empty trough/outer tray on dry kitchen paper inside an existing dish. Add a modest amount of water below the growing surface. Inspect after 30 minutes and again later that day. Any wet patch underneath fails the test: use another dish for growing while repairing/reprinting. The 30-minute check is our proposed initial screen, not a leak certification. PLA prints may retain residue and are not established food-contact equipment. Treat unknown-filament prints as growth/mechanical tests; use a suitable food-growing container for any batch intended to eat. Avoid boiling water or a hot dishwasher on the PLA parts. Make the wick actually touch the water For the rectangular planter: snap its four insets into the holder. Feed paper down into each inset and lay 3–4 layers across the seed platform, maintaining a continuous wet-paper path. Pre-wet the paper, drain surface puddles and fill the trough below the seed platform. The creator suggests about 80% full; don’t use that as an excuse to submerge seeds. For the square kit: put damp paper on the perforated insert inside its outer tray. Keep it moist from above initially; only rely on bottom water after confirming paper/root contact or a working wick. Water underneath an air gap cannot wet the paper automatically. Sow a small, even patch Scatter dry cress seeds onto moist paper, with no thick piles. Do not pre-soak cress: it becomes sticky when wet. One packet is enough for small test patches; there is no need to densely fill the entire large tray. Give both kits similar seeded patch areas and density, using the same seed lot. Keep an unseeded edge on the same sheet for moisture checks. Use a phone note or tape already at home to label A = wick planter, B = square tray, and optionally C = household dish. A household reference can help distinguish seed trouble from a printed-container problem; it is not a controlled scientific experiment. Keep the first stage damp, then give it light Follow the seed packet’s conditions. A loose cover can reduce early drying; check at least morning and evening and do not seal it airtight. Remove the cover when shoots emerge and begin standing up; use the plant’s condition rather than an automatic date. title: Rectangular self-watering cress planter
text: Rectangular self-watering cress planter 6 printed pieces What each piece does Trough: stores the small supply of water. Holder: supports the growing paper above it. title: How the robot joins this later
text: How the robot joins this later Recognize the tray and the saved watering target while its base is parked. Inspect the uncovered crop; a person checks water reserve and wetness at an unseeded paper edge. The contact probe is optional. Use one removable light paddle at plant height as a separate operation. Take a small bottle, pour a tested amount at an accessible target and return upright. Observe wetness/spills and save evidence. Uncertain delivery pauses the cycle. Manual lid removal, bottle refill and tool loading are acceptable V0 steps. The cress refill hole is narrow; the square tray’s access around its fitted insert also needs physical testing. Neither a render nor the upstream demo proves these targets are reachable with our bottle. Why a water pocket if the robot waters? The pocket is inside the planter; the robot can refill it. We removed the separate powered irrigation system, not the plant’s ability to hold water.

title: Where the trial stands
text: Where the trial stands September 26: the planned New York pre-trial did not happen. The K1 Max jammed with PLA in the nozzle after the first job was aborted, so no planter part is available and no leak, wick or germination test has been run. The cress seed packet was added to the cart but its purchase is unconfirmed. Everything below is a plan for the first trial, not a record of one. Garden cress ( Lepidium sativum ) suits a small paper-based trial. A seed supplier gives roughly 2–4 days to germinate and 7–10 days to harvest ; real timing varies. Seedmart’s cress guide . This is a planning estimate, not a guarantee for any particular packet. If the kits are not printed by sowing day: use a shallow household dish with household paper. The robot software does not depend on the printed geometry for its first supervised pours; it depends on a tray in a repeatable position with a visible refill opening. Seeds must be bought locally in Japan; carrying seed or growing material through customs is not planned.

title: Your first setup, step by step
text: Your first setup, step by step No moisture electronics are required: check water reserve and paper wetness by hand for this trial. Why we recommend deferring the soil probe . Use what you already have The printed cress planter or square kit once they exist; otherwise a shallow household dish. Fresh garden-cress seed. Use untreated seed intended for growing; check the delivered packet. Plain, unscented household kitchen paper and clean water. A clean kitchen tray/dish underneath, a small cup or spoon, and a phone camera. A household loose cover if the cress planter needs humidity retention; square kit includes its cover. No growing soil, fertilizer, purchased mats, sensors or robot needed for this short paper trial. What “self-watering” means The rectangular planter stores a little water below the seeds. Paper carries it upward by capillary action. You still check it and refill by hand. The square kit has a cover and removable insert, but it does not automatically wick unless its growing medium makes the needed connection to water. See the planter renders Inspect, rinse and leak-test Remove loose plastic, rinse with cool water and check the fit without forcing clips. Put the empty trough/outer tray on dry kitchen paper inside an existing dish. Add a modest amount of water below the growing surface. Inspect after 30 minutes and again later that day. Any wet patch underneath fails the test: use another dish for growing while repairing/reprinting. The 30-minute check is our proposed initial screen, not a leak certification. PLA prints may retain residue and are not established food-contact equipment. Treat unknown-filament prints as growth/mechanical tests; use a suitable food-growing container for any batch intended to eat. Avoid boiling water or a hot dishwasher on the PLA parts. Make the wick actually touch the water For the rectangular planter: snap its four insets into the holder. Feed paper down into each inset and lay 3–4 layers across the seed platform, maintaining a continuous wet-paper path. Pre-wet the paper, drain surface puddles and fill the trough below the seed platform. The creator suggests about 80% full; don’t use that as an excuse to submerge seeds. For the square kit: put damp paper on the perforated insert inside its outer tray. Keep it moist from above initially; only rely on bottom water after confirming paper/root contact or a working wick. Water underneath an air gap cannot wet the paper automatically. Sow a small, even patch Scatter dry cress seeds onto moist paper, with no thick piles. Do not pre-soak cress: it becomes sticky when wet. One packet is enough for small test patches; there is no need to densely fill the entire large tray. Give both kits similar seeded patch areas and density, using the same seed lot. Keep an unseeded edge on the same sheet for moisture checks. Use a phone note or tape already at home to label A = wick planter, B = square tray, and optionally C = household dish. A household reference can help distinguish seed trouble from a printed-container problem; it is not a controlled scientific experiment. Keep the first stage damp, then give it light Follow the seed packet’s conditions. A loose cover can reduce early drying; check at least morning and evening and do not seal it airtight. Remove the cover when shoots emerge and begin standing up; use the plant’s condition rather than an automatic date.
